quotes.quote: On this point, however, we dwell no longer, since it is the same Paul who, in his Epistle to the Galatians, counts heresies among the sins of the flesh, who also intimates to Titus, that a man who is a heretic must be rejected after the first admonition, on the ground that he that is such is perverted, and commits sin, as a self-condemned man. Indeed, in almost every epistle, when enjoining on us (the duty) of avoiding false doctrines, he sharply condemns heresies.
quotes.highlight_phrase: since it is the same Paul who, in his Epistle to the Galatians, counts heresies among the sins of the flesh
quotes.note: In his foundational North African treatise on apostolic tradition, Tertullian directly appeals to Paul's warning in Galatians 5:20 classifying heresies among the works of the flesh.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Moreover, in the Epistle to the Galatians, Paul states that Peter, still from fear of the Jews, ceased upon the arrival of James to eat with the Gentiles, and separated himself from them, fearing them that were of the circumcision; and the rest of the Jews, and Barnabas also, followed the same course.
quotes.highlight_phrase: in the Epistle to the Galatians, Paul states
quotes.note: In his mid-third-century apologetic treatise from Alexandria, Origen cites Paul by name as the author of the Epistle to the Galatians regarding the Antioch incident.

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew

quotes.quote: And James is he whom Paul says in the Epistle to the Galatians that he saw, But other of the Apostles saw I none, save James the Lord's brother.
quotes.highlight_phrase: whom Paul says in the Epistle to the Galatians
quotes.note: Writing in his commentary on Matthew, Origen of Alexandria explicitly attributes the autobiographical account in Galatians 1:19 to the Apostle Paul.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: In like manner, Paul to the Galatians: Abraham believed in God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. You know, therefore, that they which are of faith, the same are children of Abraham. But the Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the heathens by faith, foretold to Abraham that all nations should be blessed in him. Therefore they who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In like manner, Paul to the Galatians
quotes.note: In his third-century scriptural compilation from Carthage, Bishop Cyprian explicitly cites Paul's Epistle to the Galatians to demonstrate that gentiles are justified by faith.

quotes.quote: Also in the Epistle of Paul to the Galatians: If I wished to please men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Also in the Epistle of Paul to the Galatians
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the mid-third century, Cyprian of Carthage formally cites Galatians 1:10 under the title of Paul's Epistle to the Galatians.

Victorinus of Pettau.apostolic_link: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian.
Victorinus of Pettau.note: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian. — Poetovio, Pannonia (Slovenia)

quotes.quote: In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians
quotes.note: Writing in Pannonia during the late third century, Victorinus enumerates the seven churches addressed by Paul, explicitly confirming the canonical status of Galatians in the Western provinces.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: Summarizing the canonical consensus of the early fourth-century church from the library of Caesarea, Eusebius records that Paul's epistles were universally recognized and undisputed.

quotes.quote: The names of the apostles of our Saviour are known to every one from the Gospels. But there exists no catalogue of the seventy disciples. Barnabas, indeed, is said to have been one of them, of whom the Acts of the Apostles makes mention in various places, and especially Paul in his Epistle to the Galatians.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and especially Paul in his Epistle to the Galatians.
quotes.note: In his fourth-century ecclesiastical history composed in Caesarea, Eusebius cites Paul's Epistle to the Galatians alongside the Acts of the Apostles as an authoritative historical source on Barnabas.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: Instructing catechumens in mid-fourth-century Jerusalem, Cyril delineates the official liturgical canon read in the Palestinian churches, including the complete collection of fourteen Pauline epistles.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians
quotes.note: Meeting in Asia Minor during the mid-fourth century, the regional Synod of Laodicea formally catalogs the books appointed for public reading, explicitly listing Paul's Epistle to the Galatians.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians
quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius of Alexandria defines the exact twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, placing Galatians fourth among the fourteen epistles of Paul.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: Since Paul then saw the whole Galatian people in a state of excitement, a flame kindled against their Church, and the edifice shaken and tottering to its fall, filled with the mixed feelings of just anger and despondency, (which he has expressed in the words, I could wish to be present with you now, and to change my voice, ) he writes the Epistle as an answer to these charges. This is his aim from the very commencement, for the underminers of his reputation had said, The others were disciples of Christ but this man of the Apostles. Wherefore he begins thus, Paul, an Apostle not from men, neither through man.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Since Paul then saw the whole Galatian people in a state of excitement, a flame kindled against their Church
quotes.note: Introducing his commentary on Galatians in Antioch, John Chrysostom explains the urgent historical occasion that prompted Paul to open the letter with a direct defense of his apostolic commission.

quotes.quote: Thus taught, and walking in the steps of his Master, Paul has varied his discourse according to the need of his disciples, at one time using knife and cautery, at another, applying mild remedies. To the Corinthians he says, What will you? Shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in a spirit of meekness? but to the Galatians, O foolish Galatians.
quotes.highlight_phrase: but to the Galatians, O foolish Galatians.
quotes.note: Opening his fourth-century homilies on Galatians in Antioch, John Chrysostom contrasts Paul's pastoral tone toward the Corinthians with his direct rebuke to the churches of Galatia.

quotes.quote: In thus saluting all through the Epistle addressed to the Corinthians, he would at once honor these, and bring together the whole nation. But he calls them saints, thereby implying that if any be an impure person, he has no share in this salutation. But why, writing to the mother city, does he address all through her, since he does not so everywhere? For instance, in his Epistle to the Thessalonians he addressed not the Macedonians also; and in like manner in that to the Ephesians he does not include all Asia; neither was that to the Romans written to those also who dwell in Italy. But in this Epistle he does so; and in that to the Galatians. For there also he writes not to one city, or two, or three, but to all who are scattered every where, saying, Paul an Apostle, (not from men neither through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, Who raised Him from the dead,) and all the brethren which are with me, unto the Churches of Galatia. Grace to you and peace. To the Hebrews also he writes one Epistle to all collectively; not distinguishing them into their several cities. What then can be the reason of this? Because, as I think, in this case all were involved in one common disorder, wherefore also he addresses them in common, as needing one common remedy. For the Galatians were all of them infected. So too were the Hebrews, and so I think these (Achaians) also.
quotes.highlight_phrase: in that to the Galatians. For there also he writes not to one city, or two, or three, but to all who are scattered every where, saying, Paul an Apostle
quotes.note: John Chrysostom observes that Paul uniquely addressed Galatians to an entire Roman province of churches rather than a single city because the whole region shared the same doctrinal crisis.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one
quotes.note: In his fourth-century biographical catalog of Christian writers, the biblical scholar Jerome records Paul's martyrdom in Rome under Nero and enumerates his epistles, including the letter to the Galatians.

quotes.quote: He it is of whom the apostle Paul writes to the Galatians that No one else of the apostles did I see except James the brother of the Lord, and shortly after the event the Acts of the apostles bear witness to the matter.
quotes.highlight_phrase: of whom the apostle Paul writes to the Galatians
quotes.note: In his fourth-century biographical entry on James the Just, Jerome explicitly cites the Apostle Paul's statement in the Epistle to the Galatians as historical testimony.

quotes.quote: I, Jerome, son of Eusebius, of the city of Strido, which is on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia and was overthrown by the Goths, up to the present year, that is, the fourteenth of the Emperor Theodosius, have written the following: Life of Paul the monk, one book of Letters to different persons, an Exhortation to Heliodorus, Controversy of Luciferianus and Orthodoxus, Chronicle of universal history, 28 homilies of Origen on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which I translated from Greek into Latin, On the Seraphim, On Osanna, On the prudent and the prodigal sons, On three questions of the ancient law, Homilies on the Song of Songs two, Against Helvidius, On the perpetual virginity of Mary, To Eustochius, On maintaining virginity, one book of Epistles to Marcella, a consolatory letter to Paula On the death of a daughter, three books of Commentaries on the epistle of Paul to the Galatians, likewise three books of Commentaries on the epistle to the Ephesians, On the epistle to Titus one book, On the epistle to Philemon one, Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, one book of Hebrew questions on Genesis, one book On places in Judea, one book of Hebrew names, Didymus on the Holy Spirit, which I translated into Latin one book, Thirty-Nine Homilies on Luke On Psalms 10 to 16, seven books, On the captive Monk, The Life of the blessed Hilarion.
quotes.highlight_phrase: three books of Commentaries on the epistle of Paul to the Galatians
quotes.note: In the concluding catalog of his fourth-century biographical dictionary, Jerome records his own three-book commentary on the Epistle of Paul to the Galatians.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians
quotes.note: Representing the North African canonical consensus at the close of the fourth century, Augustine of Hippo explicitly lists the Epistle to the Galatians among the fourteen authoritative letters of Paul.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the end of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records the traditional New Testament canon received from the Fathers, including the fourteen epistles of Paul.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle to the Gentiles & Prisoner of Christ Jesus

internal_evidence.summary: Opens with Paul's apostolic greeting, identifies him as 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles' (Eph 3:1), and names Tychicus as letter-bearer (Eph 6:21).

verse_details.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints who are at Ephesus and [who are] faithful in Christ Jesus:
For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles--
Therefore I, the prisoner of the Lord, implore you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you have been called,
But that you also may know about my circumstances, how I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Some modern critics label Ephesians deutero-Pauline based on rhetorical style and lack of personal greetings.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Ephesians was designed as a circular letter to the churches of Asia Minor (hence the general tone); it is cited by Ignatius (Eph 12:2), Polycarp (Phil 1:3; 12:1), Irenaeus, Tertullian, and bound prominently in 𝔓46.

Ignatius of Antioch.apostolic_link: Direct disciple of the Apostle John; bishop of Antioch alongside the Apostles Peter and Evodius.
Ignatius of Antioch.note: Direct disciple of the Apostle John; bishop of Antioch alongside the Apostles Peter and Evodius. — Antioch, Syria

quotes.quote: You are initiated into the mysteries of the Gospel with Paul, the holy, the martyred, the deservedly most happy, at whose feet may I be found, when I shall attain to God; who in all his Epistles makes mention of you in Christ Jesus.
quotes.highlight_phrase: with Paul, the holy, the martyred, the deservedly most happy, at whose feet may I be found, when I shall attain to God; who in all his Epistles makes mention of you
quotes.note: Writing directly to the church at Ephesus around AD 110, Ignatius of Antioch provides early Apostolic-era testimony connecting the Apostle Paul and his epistolary corpus to the Ephesian congregation.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians
quotes.note: Composed near Rome in the late second century, the Muratorian Fragment explicitly catalogs the Epistle to the Ephesians as the second of the seven church epistles written by the Apostle Paul.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: When, therefore, the mingled cup and the manufactured bread receives the Word of God, and the Eucharist of the blood and the body of Christ is made, from which things the substance of our flesh is increased and supported, how can they affirm that the flesh is incapable of receiving the gift of God, which is life eternal, which [flesh] is nourished from the body and blood of the Lord, and is a member of Him?— even as the blessed Paul declares in his Epistle to the Ephesians, that we are members of His body, of His flesh, and of His bones.
quotes.highlight_phrase: even as the blessed Paul declares in his Epistle to the Ephesians
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul around AD 180 with direct ties to Asia Minor through Polycarp, Irenaeus of Lyons explicitly quotes Ephesians 5:30 as the words of the Apostle Paul in his Epistle to the Ephesians.

quotes.quote: Just as if any one, being an apostate, and seizing in a hostile manner another man's territory, should harass the inhabitants of it, in order that he might claim for himself the glory of a king among those ignorant of his apostasy and robbery; so likewise also the devil, being one among those angels who are placed over the spirit of the air, as the Apostle Paul has declared in his Epistle to the Ephesians, becoming envious of man, was rendered an apostate from the divine law: for envy is a thing foreign to God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: as the Apostle Paul has declared in his Epistle to the Ephesians
quotes.note: In a second explicit attestation from the late second century, Irenaeus of Lyons cites Ephesians 2:2 and attributes the teaching directly to the Apostle Paul in his Epistle to the Ephesians.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: On the whole, then, if that is evidently more true which is earlier, if that is earlier which is from the very beginning, if that is from the beginning which has the apostles for its authors, then it will certainly be quite as evident, that that comes down from the apostles, which has been kept as a sacred deposit in the churches of the apostles. Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it; what utterance also the Romans give, so very near (to the apostles ), to whom Peter and Paul conjointly bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood. We have also St. John's foster churches. For although Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the order of the bishops (thereof), when traced up to their origin, will yet rest on John as their author. In the same manner is recognised the excellent source of the other churches. I say, therefore, that in them (and not simply such of them as were founded by apostles, but in all those which are united with them in the fellowship of the mystery of the gospel of Christ ) that Gospel of Luke which we are defending with all our might has stood its ground from its very first publication; whereas Marcion's Gospel is not known to most people, and to none whatever is it known without being at the same time condemned.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the early third century, Tertullian appeals to the continuous public reading of the Apostle Paul's authentic letters preserved in the apostolic church of Ephesus.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: And we say to those who hold similar opinions to those of Celsus: Paul then, we are to suppose, had before his mind the idea of no pre-eminent wisdom when he professed to speak wisdom among them that are perfect? Now, as he spoke with his customary boldness when in making such a profession he said that he was possessed of no wisdom, we shall say in reply: first of all examine the Epistles of him who utters these words, and look carefully at the meaning of each expression in them — say, in those to the Ephesians, and Colossians, and Thessalonians, and Philippians, and Romans, — and show two things, both that you understand Paul's words, and that you can demonstrate any of them to be silly or foolish.
quotes.highlight_phrase: in those to the Ephesians, and Colossians, and Thessalonians, and Philippians, and Romans, — and show two things, both that you understand Paul's words
quotes.note: Defending Christian scholarship in the mid-third century, the Alexandrian theologian Origen points critics directly to the Apostle Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians as a benchmark of apostolic wisdom.

quotes.quote: The declaration, indeed, in the Epistle to the Ephesians, We wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places, must be so understood as if we meant, I Paul, and you Ephesians, and all who have not to wrestle against flesh and blood: for such have to struggle against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, not like the Corinthians, whose struggle was as yet against flesh and blood, and who had been overtaken by no temptation but such as is common to man.
quotes.highlight_phrase: must be so understood as if we meant, I Paul, and you Ephesians
quotes.note: In his foundational third-century treatise written in Alexandria, Origen quotes Ephesians 6:12 and explicitly identifies the speaker and recipients as the Apostle Paul addressing the Ephesians.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: Moreover, too, the Apostle Paul, more openly and clearly still manifesting this same thing, writes to the Ephesians, and says, Christ loved the Church, and gave Himself for it, that He might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the Apostle Paul, more openly and clearly still manifesting this same thing, writes to the Ephesians
quotes.note: Preserved in the third-century Cyprianic correspondence, this epistle explicitly attributes Ephesians 5:25–26 to the Apostle Paul writing to the church at Ephesus.

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: 117. That there is a strong conflict to be waged against the devil, and that therefore we ought to stand bravely, that we may be able to conquer In the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians: Our wrestle is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers and princes of this world, and of this darkness; against the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places. Because of this, put on the whole armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the most evil day; that when you have accomplished all, you may stand, having your loins girt in the truth of the Gospel, putting on the breastplate of righteousness, and having your feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace; in all things taking the shield of faith, in which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians
quotes.note: Compiling scriptural testimonies in mid-third-century North Africa, Bishop Cyprian of Carthage quotes Ephesians 6:12–17 under the explicit heading of the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians.

quotes.quote: In the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians: Children, be obedient to your parents: for this is right. Honour your father and your mother (which is the first command with promise), that it may be well with you, and you may be long-lived on the earth.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians
quotes.note: Writing from third-century North Africa, Bishop Cyprian of Carthage explicitly cites Ephesians 6:1–3 as the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians in his scriptural manual.

quotes.quote: Paul the apostle to the Ephesians: Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, in which you were sealed in the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, and wrath, and indignation, and clamour, and blasphemy, be taken away from you.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul the apostle to the Ephesians
quotes.note: In his third-century compilation of biblical testimonies at Carthage, Cyprian directly attributes Ephesians 4:30–31 to Paul the Apostle writing to the Ephesians.

Victorinus of Pettau.apostolic_link: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian.
Victorinus of Pettau.note: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian. — Poetovio, Pannonia (Slovenia)

quotes.quote: In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians
quotes.note: Writing in Pannonia during the late third century, Victorinus of Pettau explicitly enumerates the Epistle to the Ephesians among the seven church letters authored by the Apostle Paul.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: Drawing upon the library of Caesarea in the early fourth century, the church historian Eusebius records that the Apostle Paul's fourteen epistles—including Ephesians—were universally recognized and undisputed.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: Delivering catechetical instruction in fourth-century Jerusalem, Bishop Cyril formally catalogs the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul as authoritative New Testament Scripture read publicly across the churches.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians
quotes.note: Assembled in Phrygia during the mid-fourth century, the Synod of Laodicea formally lists the Epistle to the Ephesians within the fourteen canonical letters of the Apostle Paul.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians
quotes.note: In his landmark AD 367 paschal letter from Alexandria, Athanasius enumerates the exact twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, explicitly attributing the Epistle to the Ephesians to the Apostle Paul.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: Paul, an Apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colossæ: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father. Holy indeed are all the Epistles of Paul: but some advantage have those which he sent after he was in bonds: those, for instance, to the Ephesians and Philemon: that to Timothy, that to the Philippians, and the one before us: for this also was sent when he was a prisoner, since he writes in it thus: for which I am also in bonds: that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. But this Epistle appears to have been written after that to the Romans. For the one to the Romans he wrote before he had seen them, but this Epistle, after; and near upon the close of his preaching. And it is evident from hence; that in the Epistle to Philemon he says, Being such an one as Paul the aged Philemon 9, and makes request for Onesimus; but in this he sends Onesimus himself, as he says, With Onesimus the faithful and beloved brother: calling him faithful, and beloved, and brother. Wherefore also he boldly says in this Epistle, from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven. For it had now been preached for a long time. I think then that the Epistle to Timothy was written after this; and when he was now come to the very end of his life, for there he says, for I am already being offered; this is later however than that to the Philippians, for in that Epistle he was just entering upon his imprisonment at Rome. But why do I say that these Epistles have some advantage over the rest in this respect, because he writes while in bonds? As if a champion were to write in the midst of carnage and victory; so also in truth did he. For himself too was aware that this was a great thing, for writing to Philemon he says, Whom I have begotten in my bonds. Philemon 10 And this he said, that we should not be dispirited when in adversity, but even rejoice. At this place was Philemon with these (Colossians). For in the Epistle to him he says, And to Archippus our fellow-soldier Philemon 2; and in this, Say to Archippus. This man seems to me to have been charged with some office in the Church. But he had not seen either these people, or the Romans, or the Hebrews, when he wrote to them.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Holy indeed are all the Epistles of Paul: but some advantage have those which he sent after he was in bonds: those, for instance, to the Ephesians and Philemon
quotes.note: Preaching in the late fourth century, John Chrysostom situates the Epistle to the Ephesians chronologically among the prison letters composed by the Apostle Paul while in Roman chains.

quotes.quote: These facts I mention, not merely as such, but with a view of showing that Paul would needs take great pains and trouble in writing to these Ephesians. He is said indeed to have entrusted them, as being persons already well-instructed, with his profoundest conceptions; and the Epistle itself is full of sublime thoughts and doctrines. He wrote the Epistle from Rome, and, as he himself informs us, in bonds. Pray for me, that utterance may be given unto me, in opening my mouth to make known with boldness the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains.
quotes.highlight_phrase: showing that Paul would needs take great pains and trouble in writing to these Ephesians.
quotes.note: In the introductory argument to his commentary on Ephesians, John Chrysostom testifies that the Apostle Paul composed this doctrinally profound letter to the Ephesians while imprisoned in Rome.

quotes.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus. Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. Observe, he applies the word through to the Father. But what then? Shall we say that He is inferior? Surely not. To the saints, says he, which are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus. Observe that he calls saints, men with wives, and children, and domestics. For that these are they whom he calls by this name is plain from the end of the Epistle, as, when he says, Wives, be in subjection unto your own husbands.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus
quotes.note: Opening his fourth-century homiletic series in Antioch, John Chrysostom quotes and expounds the epistolary prescript identifying Paul as the author addressing the saints at Ephesus.

quotes.quote: Ver. 3. As I besought you to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia. Observe the gentleness of the expression, more like that of a servant than of a master. For he does not say I commanded, or bade or even exhorted, but I besought you. But this tone is not for all: only meek and virtuous disciples are to be treated thus. The corrupt and insincere are to be dealt with in a different manner, as Paul himself elsewhere directs, Rebuke them with all authority; and here he says charge, not beseech, but charge some that they teach no other doctrine. What means this? That Paul's Epistle which he sent them was not sufficient? Nay, it was sufficient; but men are apt sometimes to slight Epistles, or perhaps this may have been before the Epistles were written. He had himself passed some time in that city. There was the temple of Diana, and there he had been exposed to those great sufferings. For after the assembly in the Theater had been dissolved, and he had called to him and exhorted the disciples, he found it necessary to sail away, though afterwards he returned to them. It were worth enquiry, whether he stationed Timothy there at that time. For he says, that you might charge some that they teach no other doctrine: he does not mention the persons by name, that he might not, by the openness of his rebuke, render them more shameless. There were in that city certain false Apostles of the Jews, who wished to oblige the faithful to observe the Jewish law, a fault he is everywhere noticing in his Epistles; and this they did not from motives of conscience, so much as from vainglory, and a wish to have disciples, from jealousy of the blessed Paul, and a spirit of opposition to him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: That Paul's Epistle which he sent them was not sufficient?
quotes.note: Commenting on the Apostle Paul's ministry in Asia Minor, John Chrysostom connects Paul's pastoral charge to Timothy at Ephesus with the written Epistle Paul sent to the Ephesian church.

quotes.quote: In thus saluting all through the Epistle addressed to the Corinthians, he would at once honor these, and bring together the whole nation. But he calls them saints, thereby implying that if any be an impure person, he has no share in this salutation. But why, writing to the mother city, does he address all through her, since he does not so everywhere? For instance, in his Epistle to the Thessalonians he addressed not the Macedonians also; and in like manner in that to the Ephesians he does not include all Asia; neither was that to the Romans written to those also who dwell in Italy. But in this Epistle he does so; and in that to the Galatians. For there also he writes not to one city, or two, or three, but to all who are scattered every where, saying, Paul an Apostle, (not from men neither through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, Who raised Him from the dead,) and all the brethren which are with me, unto the Churches of Galatia. Grace to you and peace. To the Hebrews also he writes one Epistle to all collectively; not distinguishing them into their several cities. What then can be the reason of this? Because, as I think, in this case all were involved in one common disorder, wherefore also he addresses them in common, as needing one common remedy. For the Galatians were all of them infected. So too were the Hebrews, and so I think these (Achaians) also.
quotes.highlight_phrase: in his Epistle to the Thessalonians he addressed not the Macedonians also; and in like manner in that to the Ephesians he does not include all Asia
quotes.note: Analyzing Pauline epistolary conventions, John Chrysostom contrasts the municipal scope of the Apostle Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians with his broader provincial letters to Galatia and Achaia.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one
quotes.note: In his fourth-century biographical catalog of Christian writers, the biblical scholar Jerome explicitly records the Epistle to the Ephesians among the authentic letters composed by the Apostle Paul.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians
quotes.note: Representing the North African church at the close of the fourth century, Augustine of Hippo formally lists the Epistle to the Ephesians among the fourteen canonical epistles of the Apostle Paul.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the end of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records the traditional New Testament canon, including the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul.

quotes.quote: And the Apostle Peter says of Christ, Who is on the right hand of God, seated in the heavens. And Paul also, writing to the Ephesians, According to the working of the might of His power, which He wrought in Christ, when He raised Him from the dead, and seated Him on His right hand.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And Paul also, writing to the Ephesians
quotes.note: In his late fourth-century exposition of the Creed at Aquileia, Rufinus explicitly pairs Peter's testimony with Paul writing to the Ephesians regarding Christ's exaltation.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle to the Gentiles & Founder of the Philippian Church
apostolic_chain: Polycarp of Smyrna (Letter to the Philippians 3:2)

internal_evidence.summary: Paul and Timothy address the saints at Philippi with deep affection, referencing Paul's imprisonment, Epaphroditus, and Caesar's household.

verse_details.text: Paul and Timothy, bond-servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, including the overseers and deacons:
so that my imprisonment in [the cause of] Christ has become well known throughout the whole praetorian guard and to everyone else,
But I thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my need;
All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar's household.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: None; Philippians is accepted as an undisputed genuine epistle of Paul across critical consensus.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Polycarp of Smyrna, writing directly to the Philippians c. AD 115, explicitly reminds them: 'When Paul was absent from you, he wrote you a letter, which if you carefully study, you will find to be the means of building you up in that faith' (Polycarp, Phil 3:2).

Polycarp of Smyrna.apostolic_link: Direct disciple of the Apostle John; appointed Bishop of Smyrna by the Apostles; teacher of Irenaeus.
Polycarp of Smyrna.note: Direct disciple of the Apostle John; appointed Bishop of Smyrna by the Apostles; teacher of Irenaeus. — Smyrna, Asia Minor

quotes.quote: For neither I, nor any other such one, can come up to the wisdom of the blessed and glorified Paul. He, when among you, accurately and steadfastly taught the word of truth in the presence of those who were then alive. And when absent from you, he wrote you a letter, which, if you carefully study, you will find to be the means of building you up in that faith which has been given you, and which, being followed by hope, and preceded by love towards God, and Christ, and our neighbour, is the mother of us all.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the blessed and glorified Paul. He, when among you, accurately and steadfastly taught the word of truth in the presence of those who were then alive. And when absent from you, he wrote you a letter
quotes.note: Writing directly to the church at Philippi in the early second century, Polycarp of Smyrna reminds the congregation of the letter the Apostle Paul had personally written to them.

quotes.quote: But who of us are ignorant of the judgment of the Lord? Do we not know that the saints shall judge the world? as Paul teaches. But I have neither seen nor heard of any such thing among you, in the midst of whom the blessed Paul laboured, and who are commended in the beginning of his Epistle. For he boasts of you in all those Churches which alone then knew the Lord; but we [of Smyrna] had not yet known Him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: among you, in the midst of whom the blessed Paul laboured, and who are commended in the beginning of his Epistle
quotes.note: Addressing the Philippian congregation directly, Polycarp of Smyrna recalls how the Apostle Paul labored in their midst and commended their church at the opening of his epistle to them.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians
quotes.note: Dating to the late second century, the Muratorian Fragment catalogs the Epistle to the Philippians third among the Apostle Paul's authoritative letters to seven churches.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: Inasmuch, then, as the Church offers with single-mindedness, her gift is justly reckoned a pure sacrifice with God. As Paul also says to the Philippians, I am full, having received from Epaphroditus the things that were sent from you, the odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, pleasing to God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: As Paul also says to the Philippians, I am full, having received from Epaphroditus the things that were sent from you
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul around AD 180, Bishop Irenaeus of Lyons explicitly attributes Philippians 4:18 to the Apostle Paul in his treatise refuting second-century Gnosticism.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: On the whole, then, if that is evidently more true which is earlier, if that is earlier which is from the very beginning, if that is from the beginning which has the apostles for its authors, then it will certainly be quite as evident, that that comes down from the apostles, which has been kept as a sacred deposit in the churches of the apostles. Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it; what utterance also the Romans give, so very near (to the apostles ), to whom Peter and Paul conjointly bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood. We have also St. John's foster churches. For although Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the order of the bishops (thereof), when traced up to their origin, will yet rest on John as their author. In the same manner is recognised the excellent source of the other churches. I say, therefore, that in them (and not simply such of them as were founded by apostles, but in all those which are united with them in the fellowship of the mystery of the gospel of Christ ) that Gospel of Luke which we are defending with all our might has stood its ground from its very first publication; whereas Marcion's Gospel is not known to most people, and to none whatever is it known without being at the same time condemned.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the early third century, Tertullian appeals to the church at Philippi as an apostolic repository preserving the Apostle Paul's authentic epistle.

works.title: On the Resurrection of the Flesh

quotes.quote: Concerning this expectation and hope Paul writes to the Galatians: For we through the Spirit wait for the hope of righteousness by faith. He says we wait for it, not we are in possession of it. By the righteousness of God, he means that judgment which we shall have to undergo as the recompense of our deeds. It is in expectation of this for himself that the apostle writes to the Philippians: If by any means, says he, I might attain to the resurrection of the dead. Not as though I had already attained, or were already perfect.
quotes.highlight_phrase: It is in expectation of this for himself that the apostle writes to the Philippians
quotes.note: In his early third-century treatise on the bodily resurrection, Tertullian of Carthage explicitly cites Philippians 3:11–12 as the teaching of the Apostle Paul to the Philippians.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: And we say to those who hold similar opinions to those of Celsus: Paul then, we are to suppose, had before his mind the idea of no pre-eminent wisdom when he professed to speak wisdom among them that are perfect? Now, as he spoke with his customary boldness when in making such a profession he said that he was possessed of no wisdom, we shall say in reply: first of all examine the Epistles of him who utters these words, and look carefully at the meaning of each expression in them — say, in those to the Ephesians, and Colossians, and Thessalonians, and Philippians, and Romans, — and show two things, both that you understand Paul's words, and that you can demonstrate any of them to be silly or foolish.
quotes.highlight_phrase: examine the Epistles of him who utters these words, and look carefully at the meaning of each expression in them — say, in those to the Ephesians, and Colossians, and Thessalonians, and Philippians, and Romans
quotes.note: Defending the intellectual depth of apostolic Christianity against the pagan philosopher Celsus around AD 248, Origen of Alexandria explicitly groups the Epistle to the Philippians among Paul's profound letters.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: In the Epistle of Peter to them of Pontus: For Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow His steps; who did no sin, neither was guile found in His mouth; who, when He was reviled, reviled not again; when He suffered, threatened not, but gave Himself up to him that judges unrighteously. Also Paul to the Philippians: Who, being appointed in the figure of God, thought it not robbery that He was equal with God; but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, He was made in the likeness of man, and was found in fashion as a man. He humbled Himself, becoming obedient even unto death, and the death of the cross. For which cause also God has exalted Him, and has given Him a name, that it may be above every name, that in the name of Jesus every knee should be bowed, of things heavenly, and earthly, and infernal; and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in glory of God the Father. Of this same thing in the Gospel according to John: If I have washed your feet, being your Master and Lord, you also ought to wash the feet of others. For I have given you an example, that as I have done, you also should do to others.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Also Paul to the Philippians: Who, being appointed in the figure of God, thought it not robbery that He was equal with God
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the mid-third century, Cyprian of Carthage explicitly attributes the Christological hymn of Philippians 2 to the Apostle Paul within his scriptural anthology.

quotes.quote: Also in the Epistle of Paul to the Philippians: But doing all things for love, without murmurings and revilings, that you may be without complaint, and spotless sons of God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Also in the Epistle of Paul to the Philippians: But doing all things for love, without murmurings and revilings
quotes.note: Cyprian of Carthage cites Philippians 2:14–15 by name as an authoritative Pauline epistle in his third-century North African compilation of scriptural testimonies.

Victorinus of Pettau.apostolic_link: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian.
Victorinus of Pettau.note: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian. — Poetovio, Pannonia (Slovenia)

quotes.quote: In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians
quotes.note: Writing from Pannonia in the late third century, Victorinus of Pettau enumerates the Epistle to the Philippians among the Apostle Paul's canonical letters to seven churches.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: Summarizing the consensus of the early fourth-century church in Caesarea, the historian Eusebius records that the Apostle Paul's fourteen epistles, which include Philippians, were universally known and undisputed.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: Instructing catechumens in Jerusalem around AD 350, Bishop Cyril delineates the authoritative New Testament canon and affirms the fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians
quotes.note: Convened in Phrygia in the mid-fourth century, the regional Synod of Laodicea formally lists the Epistle to the Philippians among the fourteen canonical epistles of the Apostle Paul.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians
quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367 from Alexandria, Bishop Athanasius ratifies the twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, explicitly listing the Epistle to the Philippians among Paul's fourteen letters.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: Paul, an Apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colossæ: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father. Holy indeed are all the Epistles of Paul: but some advantage have those which he sent after he was in bonds: those, for instance, to the Ephesians and Philemon: that to Timothy, that to the Philippians, and the one before us: for this also was sent when he was a prisoner, since he writes in it thus: for which I am also in bonds: that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. But this Epistle appears to have been written after that to the Romans. For the one to the Romans he wrote before he had seen them, but this Epistle, after; and near upon the close of his preaching. And it is evident from hence; that in the Epistle to Philemon he says, Being such an one as Paul the aged Philemon 9, and makes request for Onesimus; but in this he sends Onesimus himself, as he says, With Onesimus the faithful and beloved brother: calling him faithful, and beloved, and brother. Wherefore also he boldly says in this Epistle, from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven. For it had now been preached for a long time. I think then that the Epistle to Timothy was written after this; and when he was now come to the very end of his life, for there he says, for I am already being offered; this is later however than that to the Philippians, for in that Epistle he was just entering upon his imprisonment at Rome. But why do I say that these Epistles have some advantage over the rest in this respect, because he writes while in bonds? As if a champion were to write in the midst of carnage and victory; so also in truth did he. For himself too was aware that this was a great thing, for writing to Philemon he says, Whom I have begotten in my bonds. Philemon 10 And this he said, that we should not be dispirited when in adversity, but even rejoice. At this place was Philemon with these (Colossians). For in the Epistle to him he says, And to Archippus our fellow-soldier Philemon 2; and in this, Say to Archippus. This man seems to me to have been charged with some office in the Church. But he had not seen either these people, or the Romans, or the Hebrews, when he wrote to them.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Holy indeed are all the Epistles of Paul: but some advantage have those which he sent after he was in bonds: those, for instance, to the Ephesians and Philemon: that to Timothy, that to the Philippians
quotes.note: Analyzing the chronology of the Pauline prison letters in late fourth-century Antioch, John Chrysostom places the composition of the Epistle to the Philippians during Paul's imprisonment in Rome.

quotes.quote: Wherefore is it, O Paul, that, wishing to bring these Judaizers to the faith, you introduce none of those great and illustrious topics which occur in your Epistle to the Philippians, as, Who, being in the form of God, counted it not a prize to be on an equality with God, or which you afterwards declared in that to the Hebrews, the effulgence of his glory, and the very image of His substance; or again, what in the opening of his Gospel the son of thunder sounded forth, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God;. or what Jesus Himself oftentimes declared to the Jews, that His power and authority was equal to the Father's?
quotes.highlight_phrase: O Paul, that, wishing to bring these Judaizers to the faith, you introduce none of those great and illustrious topics which occur in your Epistle to the Philippians
quotes.note: Preaching in Antioch and Constantinople during the late fourth century, John Chrysostom directly links the Christology of Philippians 2 to the Apostle Paul alongside Galatians and Hebrews.

quotes.quote: The Philippians are of a city in Macedonia, a city that is a colony, as Luke says. Here that seller of purple was converted, a woman of uncommon piety and heedfulness. Here the ruler of the synagogue believed. Here was Paul scourged with Silas. Here the magistrates requested them to depart, and were afraid of them, and the preaching had an illustrious commencement. And he bears them many and high testimonies himself, calling them his own crown, and saying they had suffered much. For, To you, he says, it has been granted of God, not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer in His behalf. But when he wrote to them, it happened that he was in bonds. Therefore he says, So that my bonds became manifest in Christ in the whole prætorium, calling the palace of Nero the prætorium. But he was bound and let go again, and this he showed to Timothy by saying, At my first defense no one took my part, but all forsook me: may it not be laid to their account. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me. He speaks of the bonds then in which he was before that defense. For that Timothy was not present then, is evident: for, At my first defense, he says, no man took my part; and this, by writing, he was making known to him. He would not then, had he already known it, have written thus to him. But when he wrote this epistle, Timothy was with him. And he shows it by what he says: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy shortly unto you.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But when he wrote to them, it happened that he was in bonds.
quotes.note: In the introductory argument to his homilies on Philippians, John Chrysostom details the Macedonian background of the Philippian church and explains that Paul composed the epistle while imprisoned under Nero with Timothy present.

quotes.quote: But the Philippians had sent to him Epaphroditus, to carry him money, and to know the things concerning him, for they were most lovingly disposed toward him. For that they sent, hear himself, saying, I have all things, and abound; I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things that came from you. At the same time they sent to know this. For that they sent also to know this he shows at once in the beginning of the epistle, writing of his own matters, and saying, But I would have you know that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the progress of the Gospel. And again, I hope to send Timothy shortly unto you, that I also may be of good comfort when I know your state. This, that I also, is as if he meant as you for full assurance sent to know the things concerning me, so 'I also,' that I may be of good comfort when I know the things concerning you.
