Since then they had also been a long time without sending (for this he proves by saying, Now at length you have revived your thought for me ), and then they heard that he was in bonds; for if they heard about Epaphroditus, that he was sick, he being no such very remarkable person as Paul was, much more did they hear about Paul, and it was reasonable that they should be disturbed; therefore, in the opening of the epistle he offers them much consolation about his bonds, showing that they should not merely not be disturbed, but even rejoice.
quotes.highlight_phrase: in the opening of the epistle he offers them much consolation about his bonds
quotes.note: Continuing his prologue to the epistle, John Chrysostom explains that the Philippians had sent Epaphroditus with financial aid to the imprisoned Apostle Paul, prompting Paul to write this letter of consolation and gratitude.

quotes.quote: Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, fellow-Bishops and Deacons: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. Here, as writing to those of equal honor, he does not set down his rank of Teacher, but another, and that a great one. And what is that? He calls himself a servant, and not an Apostle.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, fellow-Bishops and Deacons
quotes.note: In the opening of his homiletic commentary on Philippians, John Chrysostom quotes the epistle's prescript naming Paul and Timothy and examines Paul's deliberate choice of title.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of early Christian writers composed at Bethlehem in AD 392, Jerome records that the Apostle Paul authored the Epistle to the Philippians among his letters to seven churches.

quotes.quote: Clement, of whom the apostle Paul writing to the Philippians says With Clement and others of my fellow-workers whose names are written in the book of life, the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter, if indeed the second was Linus and the third Anacletus, although most of the Latins think that Clement was second after the apostle. He wrote, on the part of the church of Rome, an especially valuable Letter to the church of the Corinthians, which in some places is publicly read, and which seems to me to agree in style with the epistle to the Hebrews which passes under the name of Paul but it differs from this same epistle, not only in many of its ideas, but also in respect of the order of words, and its likeness in either respect is not very great.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Clement, of whom the apostle Paul writing to the Philippians says With Clement and others of my fellow-workers
quotes.note: In his biography of Clement of Rome, Jerome identifies Bishop Clement as the apostolic coworker whom the Apostle Paul commends by name in his Epistle to the Philippians.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa at the end of the fourth century, Augustine of Hippo enumerates the Epistle to the Philippians among the fourteen canonical letters of the Apostle Paul.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul
quotes.note: Recording the Latin canonical tradition of Aquileia around AD 404, Rufinus affirms the fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul as the received New Testament canon of the Fathers.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle to the Gentiles

internal_evidence.summary: Opens with Paul and Timothy, intertwines closely with the personal personnel of Philemon (Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Mark, Luke), and concludes with Paul's personal handwriting.

verse_details.text: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother,
As to all my affairs, Tychicus, [our] beloved brother and faithful servant and fellow bond-servant in the Lord, will bring you information.
and with him Onesimus, [our] faithful and beloved brother, who is one of your [number]. They will inform you about the whole situation here.
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my imprisonment. Grace be with you.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Some critical scholars argue Colossians reflects a more developed Christology than earlier letters.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: The exact overlap of personal names with the undisputed letter to Philemon demonstrates common historical authorship and circumstances; attested by the Muratorian Canon, Irenaeus, Clement, and Tertullian.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians
quotes.note: This late second-century Roman canonical catalog explicitly enumerates the Epistle to the Colossians as the fourth church letter written by the Apostle Paul.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: That he was not merely a follower, but also a fellow-labourer of the apostles, but especially of Paul, Paul has himself declared also in the Epistles, saying: Demas has forsaken me,... and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. From this he shows that he was always attached to and inseparable from him. And again he says, in the Epistle to the Colossians: Luke, the beloved physician, greets you. But surely if Luke, who always preached in company with Paul, and is called by him the beloved, and with him performed the work of an evangelist, and was entrusted to hand down to us a Gospel, learned nothing different from him ( Paul ), as has been pointed out from his words, how can these men, who were never attached to Paul, boast that they have learned hidden and unspeakable mysteries?
quotes.highlight_phrase: And again he says, in the Epistle to the Colossians: Luke, the beloved physician, greets you.
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul during the late second century, Irenaeus explicitly attributes the Epistle to the Colossians to Paul while documenting Luke's close companionship with the apostle.

Clement of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen.
Clement of Alexandria.note: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: For Paul too, in the Epistles, plainly does not disparage philosophy; but deems it unworthy of the man who has attained to the elevation of the Gnostic, any more to go back to the Hellenic philosophy, figuratively calling it the rudiments of this world, as being most rudimentary, and a preparatory training for the truth. Wherefore also, writing to the Hebrews, who were declining again from faith to the law, he says, Have you not need again of one to teach you which are the first principles of the oracles of God, and have become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat? So also to the Colossians, who were Greek converts, Beware lest any man spoil you by philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of this world, and not after Christ, — enticing them again to return to philosophy, the elementary doctrine.
quotes.highlight_phrase: So also to the Colossians, who were Greek converts, Beware lest any man spoil you by philosophy and vain deceit
quotes.note: Writing in Alexandria around the end of the second century, Clement explicitly cites Paul's warning in Colossians 2:8 and notes that the Colossian believers were Greek converts.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: And in the writings of Paul, who was carefully trained in Jewish customs, and converted afterwards to Christianity by a miraculous appearance of Jesus, the following words may be read in the Epistle to the Colossians: Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind; and not holding the Head, from which all the body by joint and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increases with the increase of God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And in the writings of Paul, who was carefully trained in Jewish customs, and converted afterwards to Christianity by a miraculous appearance of Jesus, the following words may be read in the Epistle to the Colossians
quotes.note: In his apologetic treatise against Celsus, Origen explicitly quotes Colossians 2:18–19 as the written work of Paul following his conversion to Christianity.

quotes.quote: And we say to those who hold similar opinions to those of Celsus: Paul then, we are to suppose, had before his mind the idea of no pre-eminent wisdom when he professed to speak wisdom among them that are perfect? Now, as he spoke with his customary boldness when in making such a profession he said that he was possessed of no wisdom, we shall say in reply: first of all examine the Epistles of him who utters these words, and look carefully at the meaning of each expression in them — say, in those to the Ephesians, and Colossians, and Thessalonians, and Philippians, and Romans, — and show two things, both that you understand Paul's words, and that you can demonstrate any of them to be silly or foolish.
quotes.highlight_phrase: examine the Epistles of him who utters these words, and look carefully at the meaning of each expression in them — say, in those to the Ephesians, and Colossians, and Thessalonians, and Philippians, and Romans
quotes.note: Responding to the pagan critic Celsus in the mid-third century, Origen of Alexandria appeals directly to the Epistle to the Colossians as an authentic philosophical work of Paul.

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of John

quotes.quote: But Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: But you have come unto Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to ten thousands of angels, the assembly and church of the firstborn, who are written in heaven. And in the Epistle to the Colossians: Let no one judge you in meat and in drink, or in respect of a feast-day or a new moon, or a sabbath-day; which are a shadow of the things to come.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And in the Epistle to the Colossians: Let no one judge you in meat and in drink, or in respect of a feast-day or a new moon, or a sabbath-day
quotes.note: In his early third-century commentary on the Gospel of John, Origen cites Colossians 2:16–17 by name as the authoritative teaching of the Apostle Paul.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: Also Paul to the Colossians: Who is the image of the invisible God, and the first-born of every creature. Also in the same place: The first-born from the dead, that He might in all things become the holder of the pre-eminence.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Also Paul to the Colossians: Who is the image of the invisible God, and the first-born of every creature.
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the mid-third century, Bishop Cyprian of Carthage cites the Christological hymn of Colossians 1:15–18 directly under the name of Paul.

quotes.quote: Paul also, to the Colossians: You are circumcised with the circumcision not made with hands in the putting off of the flesh, but with the circumcision of Christ.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul also, to the Colossians: You are circumcised with the circumcision not made with hands in the putting off of the flesh, but with the circumcision of Christ.
quotes.note: In his third-century scriptural compendium compiled at Carthage, Cyprian explicitly attributes the teaching on spiritual circumcision in Colossians 2:11 to the Apostle Paul.

quotes.quote: 120. That we are to be urgent in prayers In the Epistle of Paul to the Colossians: Be instant in prayer, and watch therein.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In the Epistle of Paul to the Colossians: Be instant in prayer, and watch therein.
quotes.note: In the third book of his scriptural testimonies, Cyprian of Carthage cites Colossians 4:2 as an authoritative exhortation from the Epistle of Paul to the Colossians.

Victorinus of Pettau.apostolic_link: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian.
Victorinus of Pettau.note: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian. — Poetovio, Pannonia (Slovenia)

quotes.quote: In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians
quotes.note: Writing in Pannonia during the late third century, Victorinus enumerates the seven churches addressed by Paul and explicitly includes the Epistle to the Colossians.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: Writing in early fourth-century Caesarea with access to its extensive ecclesiastical library, Eusebius records that Paul's epistles were universally recognized and undisputed across the churches.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: In his fourth-century catechetical lectures delivered in Jerusalem, Cyril formally instructs catechumens to receive the fourteen Epistles of Paul as authoritative canonical Scripture.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians
quotes.note: Assembled in Phrygia within the immediate geographical region of Colossae, the fourth-century Synod of Laodicea formally lists the Epistle to the Colossians among Paul's canonical letters.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians
quotes.note: In his landmark 367 AD paschal letter from Alexandria, Athanasius enumerates the exact twenty-seven-book New Testament canon and explicitly includes Paul's Epistle to the Colossians.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: Paul, an Apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colossæ: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father. Holy indeed are all the Epistles of Paul: but some advantage have those which he sent after he was in bonds: those, for instance, to the Ephesians and Philemon: that to Timothy, that to the Philippians, and the one before us: for this also was sent when he was a prisoner, since he writes in it thus: for which I am also in bonds: that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. But this Epistle appears to have been written after that to the Romans. For the one to the Romans he wrote before he had seen them, but this Epistle, after; and near upon the close of his preaching. And it is evident from hence; that in the Epistle to Philemon he says, Being such an one as Paul the aged Philemon 9, and makes request for Onesimus; but in this he sends Onesimus himself, as he says, With Onesimus the faithful and beloved brother: calling him faithful, and beloved, and brother. Wherefore also he boldly says in this Epistle, from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven. For it had now been preached for a long time. I think then that the Epistle to Timothy was written after this; and when he was now come to the very end of his life, for there he says, for I am already being offered; this is later however than that to the Philippians, for in that Epistle he was just entering upon his imprisonment at Rome. But why do I say that these Epistles have some advantage over the rest in this respect, because he writes while in bonds? As if a champion were to write in the midst of carnage and victory; so also in truth did he. For himself too was aware that this was a great thing, for writing to Philemon he says, Whom I have begotten in my bonds. Philemon 10 And this he said, that we should not be dispirited when in adversity, but even rejoice. At this place was Philemon with these (Colossians). For in the Epistle to him he says, And to Archippus our fellow-soldier Philemon 2; and in this, Say to Archippus. This man seems to me to have been charged with some office in the Church. But he had not seen either these people, or the Romans, or the Hebrews, when he wrote to them.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul, an Apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colossæ
quotes.note: Introducing his exegetical homilies on the letter, John Chrysostom situates Paul's composition of Colossians during his Roman imprisonment alongside the Epistle to Philemon.

quotes.quote: Paul an Apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God. It were well also to say, what from considering this Epistle we have found to be its occasion and subject. What then is it? They used to approach God through angels; they held many Jewish and Grecian observances. These things then he is correcting. Wherefore in the very outset he says, Through the will of God. So here again he has used the expression through. And Timothy the brother, he says; of course then he too was an Apostle, and probably also known to them. To the saints which are at Colossæ. This was a city of Phrygia, as is plain from Laodicea 's being near to it.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul an Apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God. It were well also to say, what from considering this Epistle we have found to be its occasion and subject.
quotes.note: John Chrysostom outlines the specific theological occasion of Paul's letter and identifies Colossae as a Phrygian city located near Laodicea.

quotes.quote: Ver. 2. And to our beloved Apphia. It seems to me that she was his partner in life. Observe the humility of Paul; he both joins Timothy with him in his request, and asks not only the husband, but the wife also, and some one else, perhaps a friend. And Archippus, he says, our fellow-soldier. Not wishing to effect such things by command, and not taking it ill, if he did not immediately comply with his request; but he begs them to do what a stranger might have done to aid his request. For not only the being requested by many, but the petition being urged to many, contributes to its being granted. And on this account he says, And Archippus our fellow-soldier. If you are a fellow-soldier, you ought also to take a concern in these things. But this is the Archippus, about whom he says in his Epistle to the Colossians, Say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it.
quotes.highlight_phrase: about whom he says in his Epistle to the Colossians, Say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord
quotes.note: Commenting on the Epistle to Philemon, John Chrysostom cross-references Paul's charge in Colossians 4:17 to identify Archippus as a minister in the Colossian church.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one
quotes.note: In his fourth-century biographical catalog of Christian writers, Jerome records Paul's martyrdom at Rome under Nero and explicitly lists the Epistle to the Colossians among his church letters.

quotes.quote: Luke a physician of Antioch, as his writings indicate, was not unskilled in the Greek language. An adherent of the apostle Paul, and companion of all his journeying, he wrote a Gospel, concerning which the same Paul says, We send with him a brother whose praise in the gospel is among all the churches and to the Colossians Luke the beloved physician salutes you, and to Timothy Luke only is with me. He also wrote another excellent volume to which he prefixed the title Acts of the Apostles, a history which extends to the second year of Paul's sojourn at Rome, that is to the fourth year of Nero, from which we learn that the book was composed in that same city.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the same Paul says, We send with him a brother whose praise in the gospel is among all the churches and to the Colossians Luke the beloved physician salutes you
quotes.note: In his biographical notice on Luke, Jerome cites Paul's greeting in Colossians 4:14 as direct Pauline testimony that Luke the physician accompanied the apostle.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians
quotes.note: Summarizing the North African New Testament canon at the turn of the fifth century, Augustine of Hippo explicitly lists the Epistle to the Colossians among Paul's fourteen letters.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the close of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records the fourteen Pauline epistles received within the ecclesiastical canon.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle to the Gentiles
book_meta.earliest_manuscripts: 𝔓46 (c. AD 175–225), 𝔓65 (3rd cent.), Codex Sinaiticus

internal_evidence.summary: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy address the church at Thessalonica shortly after Paul's initial mission, recalling their visit and persecutions.

verse_details.text: Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
For you yourselves know, brethren, that our coming to you was not in vain,
For we wanted to come to you-- I, Paul, more than once-- and [yet] Satan hindered us.
I adjure you by the Lord to have this letter read to all the brethren.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: None; 1 Thessalonians is universally recognized as one of the earliest extant Christian documents and an undisputed Pauline letter.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Widely cited from the late 1st and 2nd centuries; included in Marcion's Apostolikon and the Muratorian Canon.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction
quotes.note: Dating to the late second century at Rome, the Muratorian Fragment catalogs Paul's epistles and explicitly attests that he wrote twice to the church of the Thessalonians.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: On the whole, then, if that is evidently more true which is earlier, if that is earlier which is from the very beginning, if that is from the beginning which has the apostles for its authors, then it will certainly be quite as evident, that that comes down from the apostles, which has been kept as a sacred deposit in the churches of the apostles. Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it; what utterance also the Romans give, so very near (to the apostles ), to whom Peter and Paul conjointly bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood. We have also St. John's foster churches. For although Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the order of the bishops (thereof), when traced up to their origin, will yet rest on John as their author. In the same manner is recognised the excellent source of the other churches. I say, therefore, that in them (and not simply such of them as were founded by apostles, but in all those which are united with them in the fellowship of the mystery of the gospel of Christ ) that Gospel of Luke which we are defending with all our might has stood its ground from its very first publication; whereas Marcion's Gospel is not known to most people, and to none whatever is it known without being at the same time condemned.
quotes.highlight_phrase: what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the early third century, Tertullian appeals to the unbroken public reading of Paul's epistles in the apostolic church at Thessalonica.

quotes.quote: Come now, you who would indulge a better curiosity, if you would apply it to the business of your salvation, run over the apostolic churches, in which the very thrones of the apostles are still pre-eminent in their places, in which their own authentic writings are read, uttering the voice and representing the face of each of them severally. Achaia is very near you, (in which) you find Corinth. Since you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi; (and there too) you have the Thessalonians. Since you are able to cross to Asia, you get Ephesus. Since, moreover, you are close upon Italy, you have Rome, from which there comes even into our own hands the very authority (of apostles themselves).
quotes.highlight_phrase: Since you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi; (and there too) you have the Thessalonians.
quotes.note: Around AD 200, Tertullian testifies that the apostolic churches of Macedonia, including Philippi and Thessalonica, still preserved and publicly read the apostles' authentic epistles.

Hippolytus of Rome.apostolic_link: Leading Roman theologian and martyr; disciple of Irenaeus of Lyons.
Hippolytus of Rome.note: Leading Roman theologian and martyr; disciple of Irenaeus of Lyons. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Concerning the resurrection of the righteous, Paul also speaks thus in writing to the Thessalonians: We would not have you to be ignorant concerning them which are asleep, that you sorrow not even as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with Him. For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive (and) remain unto the coming of the Lord, shall not prevent them which are asleep. For the Lord Himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice and trump of God, and the dead in Christ shall rise first. Then we which are alive (and) remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Concerning the resurrection of the righteous, Paul also speaks thus in writing to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: Writing in Rome around AD 200, Hippolytus explicitly attributes the eschatological teaching of First Thessalonians 4:13–17 to the Apostle Paul writing to the Thessalonians.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: And as a proof that such was the apostle's meaning in writing those words which I have quoted from the first Epistle to the Corinthians, I will quote also from the first to the Thessalonians, in which Paul, as one who is alive and awake, and different from those who are asleep, speaks as follows: For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord, shall not prevent them who are asleep; for the Lord Himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: I will quote also from the first to the Thessalonians, in which Paul
quotes.note: In his mid-third-century defense of Christianity against Celsus, Origen of Alexandria explicitly cites Paul by name as the author of the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew

quotes.quote: But two made a symphony, Paul and Sosthenes, when writing the first Epistle to the Corinthians; and after this Paul and Timothy when sending the second Epistle to the same. And even three made a symphony when Paul and Silvanus and Timothy gave instruction by letter to the Thessalonians.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And even three made a symphony when Paul and Silvanus and Timothy gave instruction by letter to the Thessalonians.
quotes.note: In his Commentary on Matthew, Origen of Alexandria highlights the opening salutation of First Thessalonians, noting that Paul joined Silvanus and Timothy in writing to the Thessalonians.

quotes.quote: And Paul, in the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, testifies this concerning the Jews: For you, brethren, became followers of the Churches of God which in Judea are in Christ Jesus: for you also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they have of the Jews; who both killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, and have persecuted us; and they please not God, and are contrary to all men.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And Paul, in the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, testifies this concerning the Jews
quotes.note: Writing to the historian Julius Africanus around AD 240, Origen explicitly quotes First Thessalonians 2:14–15 as the testimony of the Apostle Paul.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: In the first Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians: That a man do not deceive his brother in a matter, because God is the avenger for all these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In the first Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: Compiling biblical proof-texts in mid-third-century North Africa, Cyprian of Carthage explicitly cites First Thessalonians 4:6 as the First Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians.

quotes.quote: And in the Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians: But we would not that you should be ignorant, brethren, concerning those who sleep, that you sorrow not as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also them which have fallen asleep in Jesus will God bring with Him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And in the Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: In his third-century scriptural compendium from Carthage, Bishop Cyprian quotes First Thessalonians 4:13–14 under the explicit heading of the Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians.

Victorinus of Pettau.apostolic_link: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian.
Victorinus of Pettau.note: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian. — Poetovio, Pannonia (Slovenia)

quotes.quote: In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians
quotes.note: Writing in Pannonia in the late third century, Bishop Victorinus of Pettau explicitly includes the Thessalonians in his canonical list of the seven churches addressed by Paul.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: Summarizing early fourth-century ecclesiastical consensus from the library of Caesarea, Eusebius records that Paul's fourteen epistles were universally recognized and undisputed across the churches.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: Instructing catechumens in Jerusalem around AD 350, Bishop Cyril delineates the official New Testament canon read publicly in the churches, including all fourteen Pauline epistles.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: The fourth-century regional council at Laodicea in Phrygia formally enumerates the canonical books of the New Testament, explicitly listing Paul's two epistles to the Thessalonians.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: In his landmark AD 367 Easter letter from Alexandria, Athanasius defines the twenty-seven-book New Testament canon and explicitly lists Paul's two epistles to the Thessalonians.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: But why does he place Silvanus before him, though he testifies to his numberless good qualities, and prefers him above all? Perhaps Timothy wished and requested him to do so from his great humility; for when he saw his teacher so humble-minded, as to associate his disciple with himself, he would much the more have desired this, and eagerly sought it. For he says, Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, unto the Church of the Thessalonians. Here he gives himself no title — not an Apostle, not a Servant; I suppose, because the men were newly instructed, and had not yet had any experience of him, he does not apply the title; and it was as yet the beginning of his preaching to them.
quotes.highlight_phrase: For he says, Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, unto the Church of the Thessalonians.
quotes.note: Introducing his commentary on First Thessalonians, John Chrysostom examines the historical circumstances of the letter's opening salutation from Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy to the newly planted church.

quotes.quote: In thus saluting all through the Epistle addressed to the Corinthians, he would at once honor these, and bring together the whole nation. But he calls them saints, thereby implying that if any be an impure person, he has no share in this salutation. But why, writing to the mother city, does he address all through her, since he does not so everywhere? For instance, in his Epistle to the Thessalonians he addressed not the Macedonians also; and in like manner in that to the Ephesians he does not include all Asia; neither was that to the Romans written to those also who dwell in Italy. But in this Epistle he does so; and in that to the Galatians. For there also he writes not to one city, or two, or three, but to all who are scattered every where, saying, Paul an Apostle, (not from men neither through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, Who raised Him from the dead,) and all the brethren which are with me, unto the Churches of Galatia. Grace to you and peace. To the Hebrews also he writes one Epistle to all collectively; not distinguishing them into their several cities. What then can be the reason of this? Because, as I think, in this case all were involved in one common disorder, wherefore also he addresses them in common, as needing one common remedy. For the Galatians were all of them infected. So too were the Hebrews, and so I think these (Achaians) also.
quotes.highlight_phrase: For instance, in his Epistle to the Thessalonians he addressed not the Macedonians also
quotes.note: Preaching in Antioch in the late fourth century, John Chrysostom compares the salutations of Paul's letters, noting that the Epistle to the Thessalonians was addressed specifically to that city.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of early Christian writers, the biblical scholar Jerome records Paul's martyrdom in Rome and enumerates his canonical letters, including two to the Thessalonians.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians
quotes.note: Writing in North Africa at the close of the fourth century, Augustine of Hippo sets forth the canonical New Testament Scriptures, explicitly listing Paul's two epistles to the Thessalonians.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul
quotes.note: Writing from Aquileia in northern Italy around AD 404, Rufinus records the established New Testament canon received from the Fathers, including the fourteen epistles of Paul.

quotes.quote: The Apostle Paul makes use of such arguments as the following in asserting that mortal flesh will rise again. But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is not Christ risen. And if Christ be not risen, our preaching is vain and your faith is vain. And presently afterwards, But now is Christ risen from the dead, the first-fruits of them that sleep. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. But every man in his own order. Christ the first-fruits, afterwards they that are Christ's at His coming, then comes the end. And afterways he adds, Behold I show you a mystery: We shall all rise indeed, but we shall not all be changed; or as other copies read, We shall all sleep, indeed but we shall not all be changed; in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. However, whichever be the true text, writing to the Thessalonians, he says, I would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning those who are asleep, that you sorrow not, as the others who have no hope.
quotes.highlight_phrase: writing to the Thessalonians, he says, I would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning those who are asleep
quotes.note: In his exposition of the resurrection of the body, Rufinus of Aquileia quotes First Thessalonians 4:13 alongside First Corinthians 15 as the teaching of the Apostle Paul.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle to the Gentiles

internal_evidence.summary: Explicitly addresses a forged letter circulating in Paul's name (2 Thess 2:2) and provides his personal handwriting sign-off as authenticating token in every letter.

verse_details.text: Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:
Now we request you, brethren, with regard to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to Him,
that you not be quickly shaken from your composure or be disturbed either by a spirit or a message or a letter as if from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand, and this is a distinguishing mark in every letter; this is the way I write.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Some scholars question 2 Thessalonians based on eschatological emphasis compared to 1 Thessalonians.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: The warning against forged letters in 2 Thess 2:2 and the handwritten authentication mark in 2 Thess 3:17 make sense only during Paul's lifetime; cited as Paul's by Polycarp (Phil 11:3), Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Tertullian.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians
quotes.note: Dating to the late second century at Rome, the Muratorian Fragment explicitly attests that the Apostle Paul wrote two canonical epistles to the church of the Thessalonians.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: Of whom also the Apostle Paul again, speaking in the second [Epistle] to the Thessalonians, and at the same time proclaiming the cause of his advent, thus says: And then shall the wicked one be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the spirit of His mouth, and destroy by the presence of His coming; whose coming [i.e., the wicked one's] is after the working of Satan, in all power, and signs, and portents of lies, and with all deceivableness of wickedness for those who perish; because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved. And therefore God will send them the working of error, that they may believe a lie; that they all may be judged who did not believe the truth, but gave consent to iniquity,
quotes.highlight_phrase: the Apostle Paul again, speaking in the second [Epistle] to the Thessalonians, and at the same time proclaiming the cause of his advent, thus says
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul around AD 180, Irenaeus of Lyons provides an explicit second-century attestation of Second Thessalonians, quoting chapters 2:8–12 by name as the words of the Apostle Paul.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: On the whole, then, if that is evidently more true which is earlier, if that is earlier which is from the very beginning, if that is from the beginning which has the apostles for its authors, then it will certainly be quite as evident, that that comes down from the apostles, which has been kept as a sacred deposit in the churches of the apostles. Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it; what utterance also the Romans give, so very near (to the apostles ), to whom Peter and Paul conjointly bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood. We have also St. John's foster churches. For although Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the order of the bishops (thereof), when traced up to their origin, will yet rest on John as their author. In the same manner is recognised the excellent source of the other churches. I say, therefore, that in them (and not simply such of them as were founded by apostles, but in all those which are united with them in the fellowship of the mystery of the gospel of Christ ) that Gospel of Luke which we are defending with all our might has stood its ground from its very first publication; whereas Marcion's Gospel is not known to most people, and to none whatever is it known without being at the same time condemned.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it
quotes.note: Writing in North Africa around AD 207, Tertullian appeals to the apostolic church of the Thessalonians as an enduring custodian of the Apostle Paul's authentic epistles.

quotes.quote: But how Paul, an apostle, from being a persecutor, who first of all shed the blood of the church, though afterwards he exchanged the sword for the pen, and turned the dagger into a plough, being first a ravening wolf of Benjamin, then himself supplying food as did Jacob, — how he, (I say,) speaks in favour of martyrdoms, now to be chosen by himself also, when, rejoicing over the Thessalonians, he says, So that we glory in you in the churches of God, for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations, in which you endure a manifestation of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be accounted worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer! As also in his Epistle to the Romans: And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also, being sure that tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope; and hope makes not ashamed.
quotes.highlight_phrase: when, rejoicing over the Thessalonians, he says, So that we glory in you in the churches of God
quotes.note: In his early third-century treatise defending Christian martyrdom, Tertullian of Carthage explicitly cites the Apostle Paul's commendation of the persecuted believers in Second Thessalonians 1:4–5.

Hippolytus of Rome.apostolic_link: Leading Roman theologian and martyr; disciple of Irenaeus of Lyons.
Hippolytus of Rome.note: Leading Roman theologian and martyr; disciple of Irenaeus of Lyons. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: And the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says: Now we beseech you, brethren, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together at it, that you be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letters as from us, as that the day of the Lord is at hand. Let no man deceive you by any means; for (that day shall not come) except there come the falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped: so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself that he is God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says
quotes.note: Writing at Rome in the early third century, Hippolytus quotes Second Thessalonians 2:1–4 verbatim as the authoritative teaching of the Apostle Paul to the Thessalonians.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul, moreover, in the second Epistle to the Thessalonians, shows in what manner there will one day be revealed the man of sin, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself that he is God. And again he says to the Thessalonians: And now you know what withholds that he might be revealed in his time. For the mystery of iniquity does already work: only he who now lets will let, until he be taken out of the way: and then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord will consume with the spirit of His mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of His coming: even him, whose cunning is after the working of Satan, with all power, and signs, and lying wonders, and with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul, moreover, in the second Epistle to the Thessalonians, shows
quotes.note: Writing in Caesarea around AD 248, the Alexandrian scholar Origen explicitly cites the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians as the work of the Apostle Paul, quoting chapters 2:3–10 at length.

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew

quotes.quote: But two made a symphony, Paul and Sosthenes, when writing the first Epistle to the Corinthians; and after this Paul and Timothy when sending the second Epistle to the same. And even three made a symphony when Paul and Silvanus and Timothy gave instruction by letter to the Thessalonians.
quotes.highlight_phrase: when Paul and Silvanus and Timothy gave instruction by letter to the Thessalonians.
quotes.note: Commenting on the Gospel of Matthew, Origen of Alexandria highlights the joint salutation of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy at the opening of the Thessalonian epistles.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: Paul to the Thessalonians: But we have commanded you, in the name of Jesus Christ, that you depart from all brethren who walk disorderly, and not according to the tradition which they have received from us.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul to the Thessalonians: But we have commanded you, in the name of Jesus Christ
quotes.note: In his mid-third-century scriptural anthology compiled at Carthage, Bishop Cyprian explicitly cites Second Thessalonians 3:6 under the heading of the Apostle Paul to the Thessalonians.

Victorinus of Pettau.apostolic_link: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian.
Victorinus of Pettau.note: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian. — Poetovio, Pannonia (Slovenia)

quotes.quote: In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: Writing in Pannonia in the late third century, Victorinus of Pettau catalogs the seven churches addressed by the Apostle Paul, explicitly including the Thessalonians.

quotes.quote: And Paul, speaking of Antichrist to the Thessalonians, says: Whom the Lord Jesus will slay by the breath of His mouth.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And Paul, speaking of Antichrist to the Thessalonians, says:
quotes.note: Writing in late third-century Pannonia, Bishop Victorinus of Pettau explicitly attributes the prophecy of 2 Thessalonians 2:8 regarding the Antichrist to the Apostle Paul.

quotes.quote: The Apostle Paul also bears witness, for he says to the Thessalonians: Let him who now restrains restrain, until he be taken out of the way; and then shall appear that Wicked One, even he whose coming is after the working of Satan, with signs and lying wonders. And that they might know that he should come who then was the prince, he added: He already endeavours after the secret of mischief — that is, the mischief which he is about to do he strives to do secretly; but he is not raised up by his own power, nor by that of his father, but by command of God, of which thing Paul says in the same passage: For this cause, because they have not received the love of God, He will send upon them a spirit of error, that they all may be persuaded of a lie, who have not been persuaded of the truth.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The Apostle Paul also bears witness, for he says to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: In the late third century, Bishop Victorinus of Pettau quotes Second Thessalonians 2:7–11 as the testimony of the Apostle Paul addressed to the Thessalonians.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: Summarizing the consensus of the early church from the library of Caesarea, the historian Eusebius records that the Apostle Paul's fourteen epistles were universally recognized and undisputed.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: Instructing catechumens in Jerusalem around AD 350, Bishop Cyril of Jerusalem delineates the official New Testament canon, including all fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: Meeting in Phrygia in the mid-fourth century, the Synod of Laodicea formally enumerates the books of the New Testament, including two epistles of Paul to the Thessalonians.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians
