quotes.note: In his Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius of Alexandria defines the twenty-seven books of the New Testament canon, explicitly listing two epistles of Paul to the Thessalonians.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: And, what was worse than all, some attempted merely to report words as if they were said by Paul, but others even to forge Epistles as written by him. On this account, cutting off all access for them, he says, Be not quickly shaken from your mind, nor yet be troubled, either by spirit, or by word, or by epistle as from us. Neither by spirit, he says, glancing at the false prophets. Whence then shall we know them, he says? For this very reason, he added, The salutation of me Paul with my own hand, which is the token in every Epistle: so I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. He does not here mean, that this is the token — for it is probable that others also imitated this — but that I write the salutation with my own hand, as is the custom also now among us. For by the subscription the writings of those who send letters are made known.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The salutation of me Paul with my own hand, which is the token in every Epistle: so I write.
quotes.note: In his introduction to Second Thessalonians, John Chrysostom explains that the Apostle Paul appended his own handwritten signature at the close of the letter to counter circulating forgeries.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of early Christian writers, the biblical scholar Jerome records that the Apostle Paul authored two canonical epistles addressed to the Thessalonians.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians
quotes.note: Writing in North Africa at the close of the fourth century, Augustine of Hippo lists the canonical New Testament books, explicitly including two epistles of Paul to the Thessalonians.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul
quotes.note: Expositing the Apostles' Creed in northern Italy around AD 404, Rufinus of Aquileia records the traditional New Testament canon handed down by the Fathers, including fourteen epistles of Paul.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle of Christ Jesus to his True Child in the Faith

internal_evidence.summary: Personal apostolic pastoral charge instructing Timothy on church leadership, false teachers, and qualifications for overseers and deacons at Ephesus.

verse_details.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus according to the commandment of God our Savior, and of Christ Jesus, [who is] our hope,
To Timothy, [my] true child in [the] faith: Grace, mercy [and] peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
I am writing these things to you, hoping to come to you before long;
but in case I am delayed, [I write] so that you will know how one ought to conduct himself in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and support of the truth.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Modern historical-critical scholars frequently dispute the Pastoral Epistles based on vocabulary and ecclesiastical organization.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Polycarp of Smyrna cites 1 Timothy 6:7 and 6:10 verbatim as apostolic authority (Phil 4:1); Irenaeus explicitly names 1 Timothy as Paul's letter in Against Heresies (Pref. 1; II.14.7), and the Muratorian Canon ratifies both letters to Timothy.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy
quotes.note: The late second-century Muratorian Canon explicitly attests that the Apostle Paul wrote two epistles to Timothy, which were universally esteemed across the Catholic Church for regulating ecclesiastical discipline.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: The blessed apostles, then, having founded and built up the Church, committed into the hands of Linus the office of the episcopate. Of this Linus, Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Of this Linus, Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy.
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul around AD 180, Irenaeus of Lyons explicitly refers to Paul's 'Epistles to Timothy' in the plural, attesting second-century recognition of both First and Second Timothy.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: To this epistle alone did its brevity avail to protect it against the falsifying hands of Marcion. I wonder, however, when he received (into his Apostolicon ) this letter which was written but to one man, that he rejected the two epistles to Timothy and the one to Titus, which all treat of ecclesiastical discipline. His aim, was, I suppose, to carry out his interpolating process even to the number of (St. Paul's ) epistles.
quotes.highlight_phrase: he rejected the two epistles to Timothy and the one to Titus, which all treat of ecclesiastical discipline.
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa around AD 207, Tertullian attests that Paul's two epistles to Timothy on church discipline belong to the authentic Pauline corpus that Marcion arbitrarily excised.

quotes.quote: Him, too, did Paul behold; but yet he saw not the Father. Have I not, he says, seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Moreover, he expressly called Christ God, saying: Of whom are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed forever. He shows us also that the Son of God, which is the Word of God, is visible, because He who became flesh was called Christ. Of the Father, however, he says to Timothy: Whom none among men has seen, nor indeed can see; and he accumulates the description in still ampler terms: Who only has immortality, and dwells in the light which no man can approach unto. It was of Him, too, that he had said in a previous passage: Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, to the only God;
quotes.highlight_phrase: Of the Father, however, he says to Timothy: Whom none among men has seen, nor indeed can see
quotes.note: In his treatise defending Trinitarian theology, Tertullian of Carthage cites Paul's doxologies in First Timothy Chapters 1 and 6 as authoritative apostolic Scripture.

quotes.quote: But here is, as we have said, the same madness, in their allowing indeed that the apostles were ignorant of nothing, and preached not any (doctrines) which contradicted one another, but at the same time insisting that they did not reveal all to all men, for that they proclaimed some openly and to all the world, while they disclosed others (only) in secret and to a few, because Paul addressed even this expression to Timothy: O Timothy, guard that which is entrusted to you; and again: That good thing which was committed unto you keep. What is this deposit? Is it so secret as to be supposed to characterize a new doctrine? Or is it a part of that charge of which he says, This charge I commit unto you, son Timothy?
quotes.highlight_phrase: because Paul addressed even this expression to Timothy: O Timothy, guard that which is entrusted to you
quotes.note: Writing in his Prescription Against Heretics around AD 200, Tertullian cites Paul's solemn charge to Timothy in First Timothy to refute Gnostic claims of secret apostolic traditions.

quotes.quote: Paul, in his first epistle to the Corinthians, sets his mark on certain who denied and doubted the resurrection. This opinion was the special property of the Sadducees. A part of it, however, is maintained by Marcion and Apelles and Valentinus, and all other impugners of the resurrection. Writing also to the Galatians, he inveighs against such men as observed and defend circumcision and the (Mosaic) law. Thus runs Hebion's heresy. Such also as forbid to marry he reproaches in his instructions to Timothy. Now, this is the teaching of Marcion and his follower Apelles. (The apostle) directs a similar blow against those who said that the resurrection was past already.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Such also as forbid to marry he reproaches in his instructions to Timothy.
quotes.note: Tertullian demonstrates that Paul's warnings to Timothy against ascetic teachers who forbid marriage directly anticipated second-century movements led by Marcion and Apelles.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: And in the Gospel according to Luke, Peter says to Jesus, Depart from me, O Lord, for I am a sinful man. Moreover, Paul, who himself also at a later time became an apostle of Jesus, says in his Epistle to Timothy, This is a faithful saying, that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Moreover, Paul, who himself also at a later time became an apostle of Jesus, says in his Epistle to Timothy
quotes.note: Defending Christianity against the pagan philosopher Celsus in the mid-third century, Origen of Alexandria quotes First Timothy 1:15 directly as the words of the Apostle Paul.

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew

quotes.quote: But, while dealing with the passage, I would say that we will be able perhaps now to understand and clearly set forth a question which is hard to grasp and see into, with regard to the legislation of the Apostle concerning ecclesiastical matters; for Paul wishes no one of those of the church, who has attained to any eminence beyond the many, as is attained in the administration of the sacraments, to make trial of a second marriage. For laying down the law in regard to bishops in the first Epistle to Timothy, he says, If a man seeks the office of a bishop, he desires a good work. The bishop, therefore, must be without reproach, the husbands of one wife, temperate, sober-minded, etc.; and, in regard to deacons, Let the deacons, he says, be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well, etc. Yea, and also when appointing widows, he says, Let there be no one as a widow under threescore years old, having been the wife of one man; and after this he says the things superadded, as being second or third in importance to this. And, in the Epistle to Titus, For this cause, he says, I left you in Crete that you should set in order the things that were wanting, and appoint elders in every city as I gave you charge. If any one is blameless, the husband of one wife, having children, that believe — of course — and so on.
quotes.highlight_phrase: For laying down the law in regard to bishops in the first Epistle to Timothy, he says
quotes.note: In his Commentary on Matthew, Origen of Alexandria explicitly cites Paul's qualifications for bishops, deacons, and widows from the First Epistle to Timothy as binding ecclesiastical law.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: But it happens, by a love of presumption and of obstinacy, that one would rather maintain his own evil and false position, than agree in the right and true which belongs to another. Looking forward to which, the blessed Apostle Paul writes to Timothy, and warns him that a bishop must not be litigious, nor contentious, but gentle and teachable.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the blessed Apostle Paul writes to Timothy, and warns him that a bishop must not be litigious, nor contentious, but gentle and teachable.
quotes.note: Writing to Bishop Pompey during the mid-third-century baptismal controversy, Cyprian of Carthage appeals to Paul's pastoral instructions to Timothy regarding the character required of a bishop.

quotes.quote: But if, further, he shall harass and provoke you with his insults, you must exercise against him the power of your dignity, by either deposing him or excommunicating him. For if the Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, said, Let no man despise your youth, how much rather must it he said by your colleagues to you, Let no man despise your age?
quotes.highlight_phrase: the Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, said, Let no man despise your youth
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the mid-third century, Cyprian cites 1 Timothy 4:12 as an authoritative directive from the Apostle Paul to Timothy regarding ecclesiastical discipline.

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: In the first Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians: Let women be silent in the church. But if any wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home. Also to Timothy: Let a woman learn with silence, in all subjection. But I permit not a woman to teach, nor to be set over the man, but to be in silence. For Adam was first formed, then Eve; and Adam was not seduced, but the woman was seduced.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Also to Timothy: Let a woman learn with silence, in all subjection.
quotes.note: In his third-century anthology of biblical testimonies compiled in North Africa, Bishop Cyprian of Carthage pairs Paul's instructions in First Corinthians with his teaching in First Timothy.

quotes.quote: In the first Epistle of Paul to Timothy: Honour widows which are truly widows. But the widow that is wanton, is dead while she lives. And again: But the younger widows pass by: for when they shall be wanton in Christ, they wish to marry; having judgment, because they have cast off their first faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In the first Epistle of Paul to Timothy: Honour widows which are truly widows.
quotes.note: In his third-century scriptural compendium from Carthage, Cyprian explicitly cites 1 Timothy 5 by its formal title as the First Epistle of Paul to Timothy.

Victorinus of Pettau.apostolic_link: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian.
Victorinus of Pettau.note: Earliest extant Latin biblical commentator; martyred under Diocletian. — Poetovio, Pannonia (Slovenia)

quotes.quote: In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: he thus says to Timothy: That you may know how you ought to behave yourself in the Church of the living God.
quotes.note: Victorinus of Pettau, writing in late third-century Pannonia, confirms Paul's authorship of First Timothy alongside his letters to the seven churches.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: In his early fourth-century ecclesiastical history, Eusebius of Caesarea records that Paul's fourteen epistles, including the Pastorals, were universally known and undisputed across the churches.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul
quotes.note: Delivering his catechetical lectures in Jerusalem around AD 350, Cyril enumerates the fourteen canonical epistles of Paul as the authoritative seal of apostolic teaching.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.note: The fourth-century Synod of Laodicea in Asia Minor formally lists Paul's two epistles to Timothy within its official catalog of canonical New Testament Scriptures.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon.
quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius of Alexandria ratifies the exact twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, explicitly including Paul's two letters to Timothy.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: The blessed John the Evangelist spent the chief part of his time there: he was there when he was banished, and there he died. It was there too that Paul left Timothy, as he says in writing to him, As I exhorted you to tarry at Ephesus.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul left Timothy, as he says in writing to him, As I exhorted you to tarry at Ephesus.
quotes.note: In his introductory argument to Ephesians, John Chrysostom connects Paul's historical ministry in Asia Minor with his explicit statement in 1 Timothy 1:3 regarding Timothy's charge at Ephesus.

quotes.quote: The affection of Paul for him is a sufficient evidence of his character. For he elsewhere says of him, You know the proof of him, that as a son with a father, he has served with me in the Gospel. And to the Corinthians again he writes: I have sent unto you Timothy, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord. And again: Let no man despise him, for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. And to the Hebrews he writes, Know that our brother Timothy is set at liberty. Indeed his love for him is everywhere apparent, and the miracles that are now wrought still attest his claims. 2. If it should be asked why he addresses Epistles to Titus and Timothy alone, though Silas was approved, as also was Luke, for he writes, Only Luke is with me, and Clement was one of his associates, of whom he says, with Clement and other my fellow-laborers, for what reason then does he write only to Titus and Timothy? It is because he had already committed the care of churches to these, and certain marked places had been assigned to them, but the others were in attendance upon him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: for what reason then does he write only to Titus and Timothy? It is because he had already committed the care of churches to these
quotes.note: In his introductory argument to First Timothy, John Chrysostom explains that Paul addressed pastoral epistles specifically to Timothy and Titus because he had entrusted them with episcopal oversight of local churches.

quotes.quote: Ver. 3. As I besought you to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia. Observe the gentleness of the expression, more like that of a servant than of a master. For he does not say I commanded, or bade or even exhorted, but I besought you. But this tone is not for all: only meek and virtuous disciples are to be treated thus. The corrupt and insincere are to be dealt with in a different manner, as Paul himself elsewhere directs, Rebuke them with all authority; and here he says charge, not beseech, but charge some that they teach no other doctrine. What means this? That Paul's Epistle which he sent them was not sufficient? Nay, it was sufficient; but men are apt sometimes to slight Epistles, or perhaps this may have been before the Epistles were written. He had himself passed some time in that city. There was the temple of Diana, and there he had been exposed to those great sufferings. For after the assembly in the Theater had been dissolved, and he had called to him and exhorted the disciples, he found it necessary to sail away, though afterwards he returned to them. It were worth enquiry, whether he stationed Timothy there at that time. For he says, that you might charge some that they teach no other doctrine: he does not mention the persons by name, that he might not, by the openness of his rebuke, render them more shameless. There were in that city certain false Apostles of the Jews, who wished to oblige the faithful to observe the Jewish law, a fault he is everywhere noticing in his Epistles; and this they did not from motives of conscience, so much as from vainglory, and a wish to have disciples, from jealousy of the blessed Paul, and a spirit of opposition to him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: as Paul himself elsewhere directs, Rebuke them with all authority; and here he says charge, not beseech, but charge some that they teach no other doctrine.
quotes.note: Opening his homilies on First Timothy in Antioch, John Chrysostom examines the historical occasion of Paul leaving Timothy at Ephesus to govern the church and counter false teachers.

quotes.quote: Therefore Paul, in the beginning of this Epistle, thus expresses himself, Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God. He does not say here, Paul called, but by commandment. He begins in this manner, that Timothy may not feel any human infirmity from supposing that Paul addresses him on the same terms as his disciples.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul, in the beginning of this Epistle, thus expresses himself, Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God.
quotes.note: Opening his fourth-century homiletic commentary on 1 Timothy in Antioch, John Chrysostom expounds Paul's apostolic salutation and explains the pastoral purpose of his address to Timothy.

quotes.quote: Do you not know that bodily infirmity no less than infirmity of soul injures both us and the Church? Why, otherwise, does Paul attend to this matter, in writing to Timothy, Use a little wine for your stomach's sake, and your often infirmities?
quotes.highlight_phrase: does Paul attend to this matter, in writing to Timothy, Use a little wine for your stomach's sake
quotes.note: Preaching on the Pastoral Epistles in the late fourth century, John Chrysostom attributes the pastoral counsel of 1 Timothy 5:23 directly to the Apostle Paul writing to Timothy.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one.
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of early Christian writers, Jerome records Paul's martyrdom in Rome under Nero and enumerates his two canonical epistles addressed to his disciple Timothy.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul writes to seven churches (for the eighth epistle — that to the Hebrews — is not generally counted in with the others). He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave. Of him I think it better to say nothing than to write inadequately.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave.
quotes.note: Writing to Paulinus of Nola across his survey of the canonical Scriptures, Jerome highlights Paul's pastoral epistles instructing Timothy and Titus alongside his letters to the seven churches.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul learned the Law of Moses and the prophets at the feet of Gamaliel and was glad that he had done so, for armed with this spiritual armour, he was able to say boldly the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds; armed with these we war casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ; and being in a readiness to revenge all disobedience. He writes to Timothy who had been trained in the holy writings from a child exhorting him to study them diligently and not to neglect the gift which was given him with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. To Titus he gives commandment that among a bishop's other virtues (which he briefly describes) he should be careful to seek a knowledge of the scriptures: A bishop, he says, must hold fast the faithful word as he has been taught that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He writes to Timothy who had been trained in the holy writings from a child exhorting him to study them diligently
quotes.note: Surveying the biblical canon in his fourth-century epistle to Paulinus, Jerome summarizes Paul's pastoral instructions to Timothy in 1 Timothy 4:13–14 alongside his letter to Titus.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews
quotes.note: In his treatise on Christian instruction, Augustine of Hippo enumerates the North African New Testament canon, including two epistles to Timothy among the fourteen letters of the Apostle Paul.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the close of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records the traditional twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, including the fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle of Christ Jesus facing imminent martyrdom in Rome

internal_evidence.summary: Paul's final spiritual testament anticipating his execution ('I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race'), asking for his cloak and parchments, and noting 'only Luke is with me'.

verse_details.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus,
For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.
Only Luke is with me. Pick up Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.
When you come bring the cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, especially the parchments.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Grouped by modern critics with the disputed Pastoral Epistles.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Contains intimate, uninventible personal details (names of obscure friends like Linus, Pudens, Claudia; illness of Trophimus at Miletus); universally attested by Irenaeus (Adv. Haer. III.3.3), the Muratorian Canon, Clement of Alexandria, and Tertullian.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy
quotes.note: Dating to the late second century at Rome, the Muratorian Fragment attests that both of Paul's pastoral letters to Timothy were already revered across the universal Church for regulating ecclesiastical discipline.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: The blessed apostles, then, having founded and built up the Church, committed into the hands of Linus the office of the episcopate. Of this Linus, Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Of this Linus, Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy.
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul around AD 180, Irenaeus identifies Linus, the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, with the Linus greeted by Paul in Second Timothy 4:21.

works.title: Against Heresies (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: The blessed apostles having founded and established the church, entrusted the office of the episcopate to Linus. Paul speaks of this Linus in his Epistles to Timothy.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul speaks of this Linus in his Epistles to Timothy.
quotes.note: Preserving the original Greek text of Irenaeus's second-century treatise, Eusebius records Irenaeus's explicit attribution of the final greeting in Second Timothy 4:21 to the apostle Paul.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: To this epistle alone did its brevity avail to protect it against the falsifying hands of Marcion. I wonder, however, when he received (into his Apostolicon ) this letter which was written but to one man, that he rejected the two epistles to Timothy and the one to Titus, which all treat of ecclesiastical discipline. His aim, was, I suppose, to carry out his interpolating process even to the number of (St. Paul's ) epistles.
quotes.highlight_phrase: he rejected the two epistles to Timothy and the one to Titus, which all treat of ecclesiastical discipline
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the early third century, Tertullian testifies that both of Paul's epistles to Timothy were established ecclesiastical authorities that Marcion excised from his canon.

quotes.quote: But here is, as we have said, the same madness, in their allowing indeed that the apostles were ignorant of nothing, and preached not any (doctrines) which contradicted one another, but at the same time insisting that they did not reveal all to all men, for that they proclaimed some openly and to all the world, while they disclosed others (only) in secret and to a few, because Paul addressed even this expression to Timothy: O Timothy, guard that which is entrusted to you; and again: That good thing which was committed unto you keep. What is this deposit? Is it so secret as to be supposed to characterize a new doctrine? Or is it a part of that charge of which he says, This charge I commit unto you, son Timothy?
quotes.highlight_phrase: because Paul addressed even this expression to Timothy: O Timothy, guard that which is entrusted to you; and again: That good thing which was committed unto you keep.
quotes.note: Refuting Gnostic claims of secret apostolic traditions around AD 200, Tertullian explicitly cites Paul's exhortation in Second Timothy 1:14 as a public charge to guard the common faith.

quotes.quote: Paul, in his first epistle to the Corinthians, sets his mark on certain who denied and doubted the resurrection. This opinion was the special property of the Sadducees. A part of it, however, is maintained by Marcion and Apelles and Valentinus, and all other impugners of the resurrection. Writing also to the Galatians, he inveighs against such men as observed and defend circumcision and the (Mosaic) law. Thus runs Hebion's heresy. Such also as forbid to marry he reproaches in his instructions to Timothy. Now, this is the teaching of Marcion and his follower Apelles. (The apostle) directs a similar blow against those who said that the resurrection was past already.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Such also as forbid to marry he reproaches in his instructions to Timothy.
quotes.note: Cataloging apostolic refutations of early heresies, Tertullian cites Paul's instructions to Timothy condemning both ascetic prohibitions of marriage and the claim that the resurrection had already occurred.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: But it happens, by a love of presumption and of obstinacy, that one would rather maintain his own evil and false position, than agree in the right and true which belongs to another. Looking forward to which, the blessed Apostle Paul writes to Timothy, and warns him that a bishop must not be litigious, nor contentious, but gentle and teachable.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the blessed Apostle Paul writes to Timothy
quotes.note: In an ecclesiastical letter written around AD 256, Cyprian invokes Paul's instruction to Timothy in 2 Timothy 2:24 as an apostolic standard for episcopal conduct.

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: Of this same thing, Paul in the second Epistle to Timothy: I am now offered up, and the time of my assumption is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. There now remains for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give me in that day; and not only to me, but to all also who love His appearing.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul in the second Epistle to Timothy
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa in the mid-third century, Cyprian explicitly attributes the Second Epistle to Timothy to Paul and quotes 2 Timothy 4:6–8 as authoritative Scripture.

quotes.quote: Paul, in the second to Timothy: There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine; but according to their own lusts will heap to themselves teachers itching in hearing, tickling their ears; and shall turn away their hearing indeed from the truth, but they shall be converted unto fables.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul, in the second to Timothy
quotes.note: Cyprian of Carthage again cites the Second Epistle to Timothy by name as the work of Paul, quoting 2 Timothy 4:3–4 in his third-century scriptural compendium.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Under him Paul, having made his defense, was sent bound to Rome. Aristarchus was with him, whom he also somewhere in his epistles quite naturally calls his fellow-prisoner. And Luke, who wrote the Acts of the Apostles, brought his history to a close at this point, after stating that Paul spent two whole years at Rome as a prisoner at large, and preached the word of God without restraint. Thus after he had made his defense it is said that the apostle was sent again upon the ministry of preaching, and that upon coming to the same city a second time he suffered martyrdom. In this imprisonment he wrote his second epistle to Timothy, in which he mentions his first defense and his impending death.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In this imprisonment he wrote his second epistle to Timothy, in which he mentions his first defense and his impending death.
quotes.note: Drawing upon earlier ecclesiastical traditions at Caesarea, Eusebius records that Paul composed the Second Epistle to Timothy during his second Roman imprisonment shortly before his martyrdom.

quotes.quote: As to the rest of his followers, Paul testifies that Crescens was sent to Gaul; but Linus, whom he mentions in the Second Epistle to Timothy as his companion at Rome, was Peter's successor in the episcopate of the church there, as has already been shown.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul testifies that Crescens was sent to Gaul; but Linus, whom he mentions in the Second Epistle to Timothy as his companion at Rome
quotes.note: Recording early church history in Caesarea, Eusebius attests that Paul wrote the Second Epistle to Timothy from Rome while accompanied by Linus, the first bishop after Peter.

quotes.quote: In his second epistle to Timothy, moreover, he indicates that Luke was with him when he wrote, but at his first defense not even he. Whence it is probable that Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles at that time, continuing his history down to the period when he was with Paul. 7. But these things have been adduced by us to show that Paul's martyrdom did not take place at the time of that Roman sojourn which Luke records.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In his second epistle to Timothy, moreover, he indicates that Luke was with him when he wrote
quotes.note: Eusebius cross-references internal historical details from Paul's Second Epistle to Timothy—specifically Luke's presence at Rome—to reconstruct the chronology of Paul's final imprisonment and the composition of Acts.

quotes.quote: After the martyrdom of Paul and of Peter, Linus was the first to obtain the episcopate of the church at Rome. Paul mentions him, when writing to Timothy from Rome, in the salutation at the end of the epistle.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul mentions him, when writing to Timothy from Rome, in the salutation at the end of the epistle.
quotes.note: Eusebius identifies Linus, the first bishop of Rome after Peter and Paul, with the Linus named in the closing Roman salutation of Paul's Second Epistle to Timothy.

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: In his formal survey of the New Testament canon, Eusebius attests that the fourteen epistles of the Pauline corpus were universally acknowledged across the churches.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: Instructing catechumens at Jerusalem around AD 350, Cyril enumerates the fourteen epistles of Paul as the authoritative seal of the New Testament canon read publicly in the churches.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.note: Promulgated in Phrygia during the mid-fourth century, the conciliar catalog of Laodicea formally lists two epistles to Timothy among the fourteen canonical letters of Paul.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon.
quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius of Alexandria ratifies the twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, explicitly including both epistles to Timothy among Paul's fourteen letters.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: Paul, an Apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colossæ: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father. Holy indeed are all the Epistles of Paul: but some advantage have those which he sent after he was in bonds: those, for instance, to the Ephesians and Philemon: that to Timothy, that to the Philippians, and the one before us: for this also was sent when he was a prisoner, since he writes in it thus: for which I am also in bonds: that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. But this Epistle appears to have been written after that to the Romans. For the one to the Romans he wrote before he had seen them, but this Epistle, after; and near upon the close of his preaching. And it is evident from hence; that in the Epistle to Philemon he says, Being such an one as Paul the aged Philemon 9, and makes request for Onesimus; but in this he sends Onesimus himself, as he says, With Onesimus the faithful and beloved brother: calling him faithful, and beloved, and brother. Wherefore also he boldly says in this Epistle, from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven. For it had now been preached for a long time. I think then that the Epistle to Timothy was written after this; and when he was now come to the very end of his life, for there he says, for I am already being offered; this is later however than that to the Philippians, for in that Epistle he was just entering upon his imprisonment at Rome. But why do I say that these Epistles have some advantage over the rest in this respect, because he writes while in bonds? As if a champion were to write in the midst of carnage and victory; so also in truth did he. For himself too was aware that this was a great thing, for writing to Philemon he says, Whom I have begotten in my bonds. Philemon 10 And this he said, that we should not be dispirited when in adversity, but even rejoice. At this place was Philemon with these (Colossians). For in the Epistle to him he says, And to Archippus our fellow-soldier Philemon 2; and in this, Say to Archippus. This man seems to me to have been charged with some office in the Church. But he had not seen either these people, or the Romans, or the Hebrews, when he wrote to them.
quotes.highlight_phrase: I think then that the Epistle to Timothy was written after this; and when he was now come to the very end of his life
quotes.note: Analyzing the internal chronology of Paul's captivity letters, John Chrysostom concludes from Second Timothy 4:6 that Paul composed the epistle in chains at Rome near the end of his life.

quotes.quote: The affection of Paul for him is a sufficient evidence of his character. For he elsewhere says of him, You know the proof of him, that as a son with a father, he has served with me in the Gospel. And to the Corinthians again he writes: I have sent unto you Timothy, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord. And again: Let no man despise him, for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. And to the Hebrews he writes, Know that our brother Timothy is set at liberty. Indeed his love for him is everywhere apparent, and the miracles that are now wrought still attest his claims. 2. If it should be asked why he addresses Epistles to Titus and Timothy alone, though Silas was approved, as also was Luke, for he writes, Only Luke is with me, and Clement was one of his associates, of whom he says, with Clement and other my fellow-laborers, for what reason then does he write only to Titus and Timothy? It is because he had already committed the care of churches to these, and certain marked places had been assigned to them, but the others were in attendance upon him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: If it should be asked why he addresses Epistles to Titus and Timothy alone, though Silas was approved, as also was Luke
quotes.note: In his prologue to the pastoral letters, John Chrysostom explains that Paul addressed epistles specifically to Timothy and Titus because he had entrusted them with regional oversight of churches.

quotes.quote: The Philippians are of a city in Macedonia, a city that is a colony, as Luke says. Here that seller of purple was converted, a woman of uncommon piety and heedfulness. Here the ruler of the synagogue believed. Here was Paul scourged with Silas. Here the magistrates requested them to depart, and were afraid of them, and the preaching had an illustrious commencement. And he bears them many and high testimonies himself, calling them his own crown, and saying they had suffered much. For, To you, he says, it has been granted of God, not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer in His behalf. But when he wrote to them, it happened that he was in bonds. Therefore he says, So that my bonds became manifest in Christ in the whole prætorium, calling the palace of Nero the prætorium. But he was bound and let go again, and this he showed to Timothy by saying, At my first defense no one took my part, but all forsook me: may it not be laid to their account. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me. He speaks of the bonds then in which he was before that defense. For that Timothy was not present then, is evident: for, At my first defense, he says, no man took my part; and this, by writing, he was making known to him. He would not then, had he already known it, have written thus to him. But when he wrote this epistle, Timothy was with him. And he shows it by what he says: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy shortly unto you.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But he was bound and let go again, and this he showed to Timothy by saying, At my first defense no one took my part
quotes.note: Comparing the historical circumstances of Philippians and Second Timothy, John Chrysostom deduces from Second Timothy 4:16 that Timothy was absent during Paul's initial trial before Nero.

quotes.quote: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Jesus Christ, to Timothy, my dearly beloved son: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. What is the reason of his writing this second Epistle to Timothy? He had said, I hope to come unto you shortly, and as this had not taken place, instead of coming to him, he consoles him by a letter, when he was grieving perhaps for his absence, and oppressed by the cares of the government, which he had now taken in hand. For even great men, when they are placed at the helm, and are charged with the direction of the Church, feel the strangeness of their position, and are overwhelmed, as it were, by the waves of business. This was particularly the case when the Gospel was first preached, when the ground was everywhere unturned, and all was opposition and hostility. There were, besides, heresies commencing from the Jewish teachers, as he has shown in his former Epistle. Nor does he only comfort him by letters, he invites him to come to him: Do your diligence, he says, to come shortly unto me, and, when you come, bring with you the books, but especially the parchments. And he seems to have written this Epistle when his end was approaching. For he says, I am now ready to be offered up; and again, At my first answer no man stood with me. To set all this right, he both offers consolation from his own trials, and also says, Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus.
quotes.highlight_phrase: What is the reason of his writing this second Epistle to Timothy?
quotes.note: In the opening homily of his commentary on Second Timothy, John Chrysostom explains that Paul wrote this final letter near the end of his life to console and summon Timothy.

quotes.quote: Some time seems to have since elapsed, and Paul, when he wrote this Epistle, appears to have been at liberty. For he says nothing about his trials, but dwells continually upon the grace of God, as being a sufficient encouragement to believers to persevere in virtue. For to learn what they had deserved, and to what state they had been transferred, and that by grace, and what had been vouchsafed them, was no little encouragement. He takes aim also against the Jews, and if he censures the whole nation, we need not wonder, for he does the same in the case of the Galatians, saying, O foolish Galatians. And this does not proceed from a censorious temper, but from affection. For if it were done for his own sake, one might fairly blame him; but if from the fervor of his zeal for the Gospel, it was not done reproachfully. Christ too, on many occasions, reproached the Scribes and Pharisees, not on his own account, but because they were the ruin of all the rest. And he writes a short Epistle, with good reason, and this is a proof of the virtue of Titus, that he did not require many words, but a short remembrance. But this Epistle seems to have been written before that to Timothy, for that he wrote as near his end and in prison, but here, as free and at liberty. For his saying, I have determined to winter at Nicopolis, is a proof that he was not yet in bonds, as when he wrote to Timothy.
quotes.highlight_phrase: this Epistle seems to have been written before that to Timothy, for that he wrote as near his end and in prison
quotes.note: Contrasting the pastoral epistles in his commentary on Titus, John Chrysostom observes that Paul composed Titus while free, whereas he wrote Second Timothy from prison near his death.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: It ought to be said that at the first defense, the power of Nero having not yet been confirmed, nor his wickedness broken forth to such a degree as the histories relate concerning him, Paul was dismissed by Nero, that the gospel of Christ might be preached also in the West. As he himself writes in the second epistle to Timothy, at the time when he was about to be put to death dictating his epistle as he did while in chains; At my first defense no one took my part, but all forsook me: may it not be laid to their account. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me; that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and that all the Gentiles might hear, and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion — clearly indicating Nero as lion on account of his cruelty. And directly following he says The Lord delivered me from the mouth of the lion and again shortly The Lord delivered me from every evil work and saved me unto his heavenly kingdom, for indeed he felt within himself that his martyrdom was near at hand, for in the same epistle he announced for I am already being offered and the time of my departure is at hand.
quotes.highlight_phrase: As he himself writes in the second epistle to Timothy, at the time when he was about to be put to death dictating his epistle
quotes.note: In his biography of the apostle Paul, Jerome testifies that Paul dictated the Second Epistle to Timothy while in Roman chains shortly before his execution under Nero.

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one.
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of Christian writers, Jerome records Paul's martyrdom under Nero at Rome and enumerates his two epistles to his disciple Timothy among his authentic letters.

quotes.quote: Luke a physician of Antioch, as his writings indicate, was not unskilled in the Greek language. An adherent of the apostle Paul, and companion of all his journeying, he wrote a Gospel, concerning which the same Paul says, We send with him a brother whose praise in the gospel is among all the churches and to the Colossians Luke the beloved physician salutes you, and to Timothy Luke only is with me. He also wrote another excellent volume to which he prefixed the title Acts of the Apostles, a history which extends to the second year of Paul's sojourn at Rome, that is to the fourth year of Nero, from which we learn that the book was composed in that same city.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and to the Colossians Luke the beloved physician salutes you, and to Timothy Luke only is with me.
quotes.note: In his biographical entry on Luke the Evangelist, Jerome cites Paul's remark in Second Timothy 4:11 to confirm Luke's steadfast companionship with the apostle at Rome.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul writes to seven churches (for the eighth epistle — that to the Hebrews — is not generally counted in with the others). He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave. Of him I think it better to say nothing than to write inadequately.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The apostle Paul writes to seven churches (for the eighth epistle — that to the Hebrews — is not generally counted in with the others). He instructs Timothy and Titus
quotes.note: Surveying the books of Scripture in his epistle to Paulinus of Nola, Jerome summarizes Paul's pastoral letters as authoritative instructions addressed directly to Timothy and Titus.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul learned the Law of Moses and the prophets at the feet of Gamaliel and was glad that he had done so, for armed with this spiritual armour, he was able to say boldly the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds; armed with these we war casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ; and being in a readiness to revenge all disobedience. He writes to Timothy who had been trained in the holy writings from a child exhorting him to study them diligently and not to neglect the gift which was given him with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. To Titus he gives commandment that among a bishop's other virtues (which he briefly describes) he should be careful to seek a knowledge of the scriptures: A bishop, he says, must hold fast the faithful word as he has been taught that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He writes to Timothy who had been trained in the holy writings from a child
quotes.note: Writing to Paulinus of Nola in the late fourth century, Jerome explicitly connects the Apostle Paul with the exhortation in 2 Timothy 3:15 regarding Timothy's childhood scriptural training.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews
quotes.note: In his treatise on biblical interpretation, Augustine of Hippo enumerates the North African New Testament canon, explicitly listing two letters to Timothy among Paul's fourteen epistles.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the close of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records the fourteen epistles of Paul as the received canon handed down by the Fathers.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle of Jesus Christ

internal_evidence.summary: Paul writes to Titus, his true child in a common faith, whom he left in Crete to set in order what remains and appoint elders in every city.

verse_details.text: Paul, a bond-servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the faith of those chosen of God and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness,
To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
For this reason I left you in Crete, that you would set in order what remains and appoint elders in every city as I directed you,
When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Modern critics dispute Pauline authorship as part of the Pastoral corpus.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Even the encratite heretic Tatian (c. 170), who rejected other Pauline epistles, defended the authenticity of Titus; Irenaeus quotes Titus 3:10 as Paul's, and early papyrus 𝔓32 (late 2nd century) contains Titus.

Tatian the Assyrian.apostolic_link: Pupil of Justin Martyr in Rome; compiler of the Diatessaron (harmony of the four Gospels).
Tatian the Assyrian.note: Pupil of Justin Martyr in Rome; compiler of the Diatessaron (harmony of the four Gospels). — Assyria & Rome

quotes.quote: Tatian, the patriarch of the Encratites, who himself rejected some of Paul's Epistles, believed this especially, that is [addressed] to Titus, ought to be declared to be the apostle's, thinking little of the assertion of Marcion and others, who agree with him on this point.— Hieron.: Præf. in Com. ad Tit.
quotes.highlight_phrase: believed this especially, that is [addressed] to Titus, ought to be declared to be the apostle's
quotes.note: Writing in the mid-second century, Tatian the Assyrian explicitly affirmed Pauline authorship of the Epistle to Titus in contrast to Marcion's truncated canon.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy
quotes.note: Dating to the late second century, the Muratorian Fragment catalogs the Epistle to Titus among Paul's authentic pastoral letters esteemed by the universal Church for regulating ecclesiastical discipline.

Clement of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen.
Clement of Alexandria.note: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Of whom four were of Asia — Thales of Miletus, and Bias of Priene, Pittacus of Mitylene, and Cleobulus of Lindos; and two of Europe, Solon the Athenian, and Chilon the Lacedæmonian; and the seventh, some say, was Periander of Corinth; others, Anacharsis the Scythian; others, Epimenides the Cretan, whom Paul knew as a Greek prophet, whom he mentions in the Epistle to Titus, where he speaks thus: One of themselves, a prophet of their own, said, The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies. And this witness is true. You see how even to the prophets of the Greeks he attributes something of the truth, and is not ashamed, when discoursing for the edification of some and the shaming of others, to make use of Greek poems. Accordingly to the Corinthians (for this is not the only instance), while discoursing on the resurrection of the dead, he makes use of a tragic Iambic line, when he said, What advantages it me if the dead are not raised? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Be not deceived; evil communications corrupt good manners.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Epimenides the Cretan, whom Paul knew as a Greek prophet, whom he mentions in the Epistle to Titus
quotes.note: Writing in Alexandria before the end of the second century, Clement explicitly cites the Epistle to Titus as the work of the Apostle Paul when discussing Titus 1:12.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: To this epistle alone did its brevity avail to protect it against the falsifying hands of Marcion.
