I wonder, however, when he received (into his Apostolicon ) this letter which was written but to one man, that he rejected the two epistles to Timothy and the one to Titus, which all treat of ecclesiastical discipline. His aim, was, I suppose, to carry out his interpolating process even to the number of (St. Paul's ) epistles.
quotes.highlight_phrase: he rejected the two epistles to Timothy and the one to Titus, which all treat of ecclesiastical discipline
quotes.note: Writing from North Africa around AD 207, Tertullian attests that the Epistle to Titus belongs to the established collection of St. Paul's letters governing church discipline.

quotes.quote: On this point, however, we dwell no longer, since it is the same Paul who, in his Epistle to the Galatians, counts heresies among the sins of the flesh, who also intimates to Titus, that a man who is a heretic must be rejected after the first admonition, on the ground that he that is such is perverted, and commits sin, as a self-condemned man. Indeed, in almost every epistle, when enjoining on us (the duty) of avoiding false doctrines, he sharply condemns heresies.
quotes.highlight_phrase: it is the same Paul who, in his Epistle to the Galatians, counts heresies among the sins of the flesh, who also intimates to Titus
quotes.note: Around AD 200 in Carthage, Tertullian cites Titus 3:10–11 directly as the apostolic instruction of Paul to Titus regarding the church's handling of heresy.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew

quotes.quote: But, while dealing with the passage, I would say that we will be able perhaps now to understand and clearly set forth a question which is hard to grasp and see into, with regard to the legislation of the Apostle concerning ecclesiastical matters; for Paul wishes no one of those of the church, who has attained to any eminence beyond the many, as is attained in the administration of the sacraments, to make trial of a second marriage. For laying down the law in regard to bishops in the first Epistle to Timothy, he says, If a man seeks the office of a bishop, he desires a good work. The bishop, therefore, must be without reproach, the husbands of one wife, temperate, sober-minded, etc.; and, in regard to deacons, Let the deacons, he says, be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well, etc. Yea, and also when appointing widows, he says, Let there be no one as a widow under threescore years old, having been the wife of one man; and after this he says the things superadded, as being second or third in importance to this. And, in the Epistle to Titus, For this cause, he says, I left you in Crete that you should set in order the things that were wanting, and appoint elders in every city as I gave you charge. If any one is blameless, the husband of one wife, having children, that believe — of course — and so on.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And, in the Epistle to Titus, For this cause, he says, I left you in Crete
quotes.note: Writing in the mid-third century, Origen of Alexandria cites Titus 1:5–6 alongside First Timothy as the Apostle Paul's authoritative legislation governing church leadership.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: In his fourth-century ecclesiastical history, Eusebius of Caesarea records that Paul's fourteen epistles—including the Pastoral Epistles—were universally recognized and undisputed across the churches.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul
quotes.note: Instructing catechumens in Jerusalem around AD 350, Cyril enumerates the fourteen canonical epistles of Paul as authoritative Scripture read publicly across the churches.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon
quotes.note: Convened in Phrygia during the mid-fourth century, the Synod of Laodicea formally lists the Epistle to Titus among the fourteen canonical letters of the Apostle Paul.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon
quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius of Alexandria defines the twenty-seven books of the New Testament canon, explicitly including Paul's Epistle to Titus.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: The affection of Paul for him is a sufficient evidence of his character. For he elsewhere says of him, You know the proof of him, that as a son with a father, he has served with me in the Gospel. And to the Corinthians again he writes: I have sent unto you Timothy, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord. And again: Let no man despise him, for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. And to the Hebrews he writes, Know that our brother Timothy is set at liberty. Indeed his love for him is everywhere apparent, and the miracles that are now wrought still attest his claims. 2. If it should be asked why he addresses Epistles to Titus and Timothy alone, though Silas was approved, as also was Luke, for he writes, Only Luke is with me, and Clement was one of his associates, of whom he says, with Clement and other my fellow-laborers, for what reason then does he write only to Titus and Timothy? It is because he had already committed the care of churches to these, and certain marked places had been assigned to them, but the others were in attendance upon him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: If it should be asked why he addresses Epistles to Titus and Timothy alone
quotes.note: Introducing the Pastoral Epistles, John Chrysostom explains why the Apostle Paul addressed personal letters specifically to Titus and Timothy as apostolic delegates entrusted with regional church oversight.

quotes.quote: Some time seems to have since elapsed, and Paul, when he wrote this Epistle, appears to have been at liberty. For he says nothing about his trials, but dwells continually upon the grace of God, as being a sufficient encouragement to believers to persevere in virtue. For to learn what they had deserved, and to what state they had been transferred, and that by grace, and what had been vouchsafed them, was no little encouragement. He takes aim also against the Jews, and if he censures the whole nation, we need not wonder, for he does the same in the case of the Galatians, saying, O foolish Galatians. And this does not proceed from a censorious temper, but from affection. For if it were done for his own sake, one might fairly blame him; but if from the fervor of his zeal for the Gospel, it was not done reproachfully. Christ too, on many occasions, reproached the Scribes and Pharisees, not on his own account, but because they were the ruin of all the rest. And he writes a short Epistle, with good reason, and this is a proof of the virtue of Titus, that he did not require many words, but a short remembrance. But this Epistle seems to have been written before that to Timothy, for that he wrote as near his end and in prison, but here, as free and at liberty. For his saying, I have determined to winter at Nicopolis, is a proof that he was not yet in bonds, as when he wrote to Timothy.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul, when he wrote this Epistle, appears to have been at liberty.
quotes.note: In his opening homily on Titus, John Chrysostom analyzes the historical circumstances of the letter's composition, noting internal evidence that Paul wrote it while at liberty before his final imprisonment.

quotes.quote: Titus was an approved one of the companions of Paul; otherwise, he would not have committed to him the charge of that whole island, nor would he have commanded him to supply what was deficient, as he says, That you should set in order the things that are wanting. He would not have given him jurisdiction over so many Bishops, if he had not placed great confidence in him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Titus was an approved one of the companions of Paul; otherwise, he would not have committed to him the charge of that whole island
quotes.note: John Chrysostom highlights the historical background of the epistle, describing Titus as a trusted companion whom Paul commissioned to oversee the churches across the island of Crete.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of early Christian writers, Jerome records the Epistle to Titus among the authentic letters written by the Apostle Paul to his disciples.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul writes to seven churches (for the eighth epistle — that to the Hebrews — is not generally counted in with the others). He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave. Of him I think it better to say nothing than to write inadequately.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave.
quotes.note: In his survey of canonical Scripture addressed to Paulinus of Nola, Jerome summarizes Paul's pastoral letters of instruction to Timothy and Titus alongside his epistles to the seven churches.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul learned the Law of Moses and the prophets at the feet of Gamaliel and was glad that he had done so, for armed with this spiritual armour, he was able to say boldly the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds; armed with these we war casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ; and being in a readiness to revenge all disobedience. He writes to Timothy who had been trained in the holy writings from a child exhorting him to study them diligently and not to neglect the gift which was given him with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. To Titus he gives commandment that among a bishop's other virtues (which he briefly describes) he should be careful to seek a knowledge of the scriptures: A bishop, he says, must hold fast the faithful word as he has been taught that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
quotes.highlight_phrase: To Titus he gives commandment that among a bishop's other virtues
quotes.note: Writing to Paulinus of Nola, Jerome cites Titus 1:9 as the Apostle Paul's direct instruction to Titus regarding the scriptural qualifications required of a bishop.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews
quotes.note: Enumerating the New Testament canon recognized across North Africa and the Western Church, Augustine of Hippo explicitly lists the Epistle to Titus among Paul's fourteen authoritative letters.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the close of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records the fourteen Pauline epistles as the received canon handed down by the Fathers.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle and Prisoner of Christ Jesus

internal_evidence.summary: Intimate personal appeal by 'Paul, an ambassador and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus' on behalf of the runaway slave Onesimus, written in Paul's own hand.

verse_details.text: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved [brother] and fellow worker,
yet for love's sake I rather appeal [to you]-- since I am such a person as Paul, the aged, and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus--
I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my imprisonment,
I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand, I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self as well).

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: In antiquity, some questioned its brevity and private subject matter rather than its authorship.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Pauline authorship is undisputed across modern and ancient scholarship; even Marcion accepted it, and Jerome and Chrysostom wrote extensive homilies defending its apostolic value.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: As to the epistles of Paul, again, to those who will understand the matter, they indicate of themselves what they are, and from what place or with what object they were directed. He wrote first of all, and at considerable length, to the Corinthians, to check the schism of heresy; and then to the Galatians, to forbid circumcision; and then to the Romans on the rule of the Oid Testament Scriptures, and also to show them that Christ is the first object in these — which it is needful for us to discuss severally, as the blessed Apostle Paul, following the rule of his predecessor John, writes to no more than seven churches by name, in this order: the first to the Corinthians, the second to the Ephesians, the third to the Philippians, the fourth to the Colossians, the fifth to the Galatians, the sixth to the Thessalonians, the seventh to the Romans. Moreover, though he writes twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians for their correction, it is yet shown — i.e., by this sevenfold writing — that there is one Church spread abroad through the whole world. And John too, indeed, in the Apocalypse, although he writes only to seven churches, yet addresses all. He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy, in simple personal affection and love indeed; but yet these are hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church, and in the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There are also in circulation one to the Laodiceans, and another to the Alexandrians, forged under the name of Paul, and addressed against the heresy of Marcion; and there are also several others which cannot be received into the Catholic Church, for it is not suitable for gall to be mingled with honey.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote, besides these, one to Philemon, and one to Titus, and two to Timothy
quotes.note: Dating to the late second century at Rome, the Muratorian Fragment provides the earliest surviving canonical catalog explicitly attesting that Paul wrote his personal epistle to Philemon, which the universal Church esteemed as authoritative.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. quotes.note: Writing in early fourth-century Caesarea, the church historian Eusebius attests that the fourteen epistles of Paul were universally recognized and undisputed across the churches, save only the debate over Hebrews.

Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.note: Meeting in Phrygia in the mid-fourth century, the Synod of Laodicea ratifies the ecclesiastical canon of Scripture, explicitly listing the Epistle to Philemon among the fourteen letters of Paul.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon.
quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367, Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria defines the exact twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, explicitly listing the Epistle to Philemon among the fourteen letters of Paul.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: Paul, an Apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colossæ: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father. Holy indeed are all the Epistles of Paul: but some advantage have those which he sent after he was in bonds: those, for instance, to the Ephesians and Philemon: that to Timothy, that to the Philippians, and the one before us: for this also was sent when he was a prisoner, since he writes in it thus: for which I am also in bonds: that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. But this Epistle appears to have been written after that to the Romans. For the one to the Romans he wrote before he had seen them, but this Epistle, after; and near upon the close of his preaching. And it is evident from hence; that in the Epistle to Philemon he says, Being such an one as Paul the aged Philemon 9, and makes request for Onesimus; but in this he sends Onesimus himself, as he says, With Onesimus the faithful and beloved brother: calling him faithful, and beloved, and brother. Wherefore also he boldly says in this Epistle, from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven. For it had now been preached for a long time. I think then that the Epistle to Timothy was written after this; and when he was now come to the very end of his life, for there he says, for I am already being offered; this is later however than that to the Philippians, for in that Epistle he was just entering upon his imprisonment at Rome. But why do I say that these Epistles have some advantage over the rest in this respect, because he writes while in bonds? As if a champion were to write in the midst of carnage and victory; so also in truth did he. For himself too was aware that this was a great thing, for writing to Philemon he says, Whom I have begotten in my bonds. Philemon 10 And this he said, that we should not be dispirited when in adversity, but even rejoice. At this place was Philemon with these (Colossians). For in the Epistle to him he says, And to Archippus our fellow-soldier Philemon 2; and in this, Say to Archippus. This man seems to me to have been charged with some office in the Church. But he had not seen either these people, or the Romans, or the Hebrews, when he wrote to them.
quotes.highlight_phrase: in the Epistle to Philemon he says, Being such an one as Paul the aged
quotes.note: Preaching in Antioch and Constantinople in the late fourth century, John Chrysostom situates Paul's letter to Philemon chronologically among the Roman prison epistles written alongside Colossians on behalf of Onesimus.

quotes.quote: Philemon was a man of admirable and noble character. That he was an admirable man is evident from the fact, that his whole household was of believers, and of such believers as even to be called a Church: therefore he says in this Epistle, And to the Church that is in your house. Philemon 2 He bears witness also to his great obedience, and that the bowels of the Saints are refreshed in him. Philemon 7 And he himself in this Epistle commanded him to prepare him a lodging. Philemon 22 It seems to me therefore that his house was altogether a lodging for the Saints. This excellent man, then, had a certain slave named Onesimus. This Onesimus, having stolen something from his master, had run away. For that he had stolen, hear what he says: If he has wronged you, or owes you anything, I will repay you. (v. 18, 19.) Coming therefore to Paul at Rome, and having found him in prison, and having enjoyed the benefit of his teaching, he there also received Baptism. For that he obtained there the gift of Baptism is manifest from his saying, Whom I have begotten in my bonds. Philemon 10 Paul therefore writes, recommending him to his master, that on every account he should forgive him, and receive him as one now regenerate.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul therefore writes, recommending him to his master, that on every account he should forgive him
quotes.note: In the historical prologue to his commentary on Philemon, John Chrysostom recounts the occasion of the letter, explaining that Paul wrote from his Roman imprisonment after baptizing the runaway slave Onesimus.

quotes.quote: Secondly, that we ought not to abandon the race of slaves, even if they have proceeded to extreme wickedness. For if a thief and a runaway become so virtuous that Paul was willing to make him a companion, and says in this Epistle, that in your stead he might have ministered unto me Philemon 13, much more ought we not to abandon the free. Thirdly, that we ought not to withdraw slaves from the service of their masters. For if Paul, who had such confidence in Philemon, was unwilling to detain Onesimus, so useful and serviceable to minister to himself, without the consent of his master, much less ought we so to act.
quotes.highlight_phrase: For if Paul, who had such confidence in Philemon, was unwilling to detain Onesimus
quotes.note: Expounding the moral lessons of the letter, John Chrysostom cites Philemon 13 to show that Paul respected Philemon's household authority by returning Onesimus with an appeal for voluntary reconciliation.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one.
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of ecclesiastical writers (AD 392), Jerome records Paul's martyrdom at Rome under Nero and enumerates his canonical letters to churches and individuals, explicitly including the Epistle to Philemon.

quotes.quote: I, Jerome, son of Eusebius, of the city of Strido, which is on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia and was overthrown by the Goths, up to the present year, that is, the fourteenth of the Emperor Theodosius, have written the following: Life of Paul the monk, one book of Letters to different persons, an Exhortation to Heliodorus, Controversy of Luciferianus and Orthodoxus, Chronicle of universal history, 28 homilies of Origen on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which I translated from Greek into Latin, On the Seraphim, On Osanna, On the prudent and the prodigal sons, On three questions of the ancient law, Homilies on the Song of Songs two, Against Helvidius, On the perpetual virginity of Mary, To Eustochius, On maintaining virginity, one book of Epistles to Marcella, a consolatory letter to Paula On the death of a daughter, three books of Commentaries on the epistle of Paul to the Galatians, likewise three books of Commentaries on the epistle to the Ephesians, On the epistle to Titus one book, On the epistle to Philemon one, Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, one book of Hebrew questions on Genesis, one book On places in Judea, one book of Hebrew names, Didymus on the Holy Spirit, which I translated into Latin one book, Thirty-Nine Homilies on Luke On Psalms 10 to 16, seven books, On the captive Monk, The Life of the blessed Hilarion.
quotes.highlight_phrase: On the epistle to Titus one book, On the epistle to Philemon one
quotes.note: In the concluding autobiographical entry of On Illustrious Men (AD 392), Jerome catalogs his own published Pauline commentaries, including his single-book commentary on the Epistle to Philemon.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul writes to seven churches (for the eighth epistle — that to the Hebrews — is not generally counted in with the others). He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave. Of him I think it better to say nothing than to write inadequately.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave.
quotes.note: Writing to Paulinus of Nola around AD 394 in a survey of all canonical Scripture, Jerome highlights Paul's personal epistles, noting specifically that the apostle intercedes with Philemon on behalf of his runaway slave.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews
quotes.note: In his treatise On Christian Doctrine (c. AD 397), Augustine of Hippo sets forth the full North African New Testament canon, explicitly enumerating Philemon among the fourteen authoritative epistles of the Apostle Paul.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy around AD 404, Rufinus of Aquileia records the received twenty-seven-book New Testament canon handed down by the Fathers, including the fourteen-letter corpus of the Apostle Paul.

book_meta.author_role: Apostolic circle associated with Paul and Timothy
book_meta.composition_date: c. AD 60–69 (Before the destruction of the Temple)
apostolic_chain: Clement of Rome / Clement of Alexandria / Origen
book_meta.earliest_manuscripts: 𝔓46 (c. AD 175–225, bound immediately following Romans among Paul's letters!)

internal_evidence.summary: Describes temple sacrifices and Levitical priesthood as actively operating in the present tense (Heb 8:4; 10:11), and references 'our brother Timothy has been set free' with greetings from 'those of Italy'.

verse_details.text: how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? After it was at the first spoken through the Lord, it was confirmed to us by those who heard,
Now if He were on earth, He would not be a priest at all, since there are those who offer the gifts according to the Law;
Every priest stands daily ministering and offering time after time the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins;
Take notice that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom, if he comes soon, I will see you.
Greet all of your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy greet you.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Critics emphasize that Hebrews is anonymous and possesses a polished Greek rhetorical style distinct from Paul's signed letters.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: The early Church carefully distinguished between the apostolic theology of Hebrews (which it recognized as inspired) and its literary amanuensis; Origen famously noted that the thoughts are the Apostle Paul's while the style may belong to Luke or Clement of Rome, and 𝔓46 places it directly in the Pauline corpus.

Clement of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen.
Clement of Alexandria.note: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Marcus, my son, salutes you. Mark, the follower of Peter, while Peter publicly preached the Gospel at Rome before some of Cæsar's equites, and adduced many testimonies to Christ, in order that thereby they might be able to commit to memory what was spoken, of what was spoken by Peter, wrote entirely what is called the Gospel according to Mark. As Luke also may be recognised by the style, both to have composed the Acts of the Apostles, and to have translated Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews.
quotes.highlight_phrase: As Luke also may be recognised by the style, both to have composed the Acts of the Apostles, and to have translated Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews.
quotes.note: In his surviving commentary fragments on First Peter, Clement of Alexandria independently confirms the Alexandrian tradition that Luke translated Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews into Greek.

works.title: Hypotyposes (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: He says that the Epistle to the Hebrews is the work of Paul, and that it was written to the Hebrews in the Hebrew language; but that Luke translated it carefully and published it for the Greeks, and hence the same style of expression is found in this epistle and in the Acts. But he says that the words, Paul the Apostle, were probably not prefixed, because, in sending it to the Hebrews, who were prejudiced and suspicious of him, he wisely did not wish to repel them at the very beginning by giving his name. Farther on he says: But now, as the blessed presbyter said, since the Lord being the apostle of the Almighty, was sent to the Hebrews, Paul, as sent to the Gentiles, on account of his modesty did not subscribe himself an apostle of the Hebrews, through respect for the Lord, and because being a herald and apostle of the Gentiles he wrote to the Hebrews out of his superabundance.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the Epistle to the Hebrews is the work of Paul, and that it was written to the Hebrews in the Hebrew language; but that Luke translated it
quotes.note: Writing in Alexandria in the late second century, Clement preserves the testimony of his teacher Pantaenus that Paul composed Hebrews in Hebrew and Luke translated it into Greek.

quotes.quote: For Paul too, in the Epistles, plainly does not disparage philosophy; but deems it unworthy of the man who has attained to the elevation of the Gnostic, any more to go back to the Hellenic philosophy, figuratively calling it the rudiments of this world, as being most rudimentary, and a preparatory training for the truth. Wherefore also, writing to the Hebrews, who were declining again from faith to the law, he says, Have you not need again of one to teach you which are the first principles of the oracles of God, and have become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat? So also to the Colossians, who were Greek converts, Beware lest any man spoil you by philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of this world, and not after Christ, — enticing them again to return to philosophy, the elementary doctrine.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Wherefore also, writing to the Hebrews, who were declining again from faith to the law, he says
quotes.note: Writing in late second-century Alexandria, Clement explicitly attributes the Epistle to the Hebrews to the Apostle Paul when citing Hebrews 5:12.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: I wish, however, redundantly to superadd the testimony likewise of one particular comrade of the apostles —(a testimony) aptly suited for confirming, by most proximate right, the discipline of his masters. For there is extant withal an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas — a man sufficiently accredited by God, as being one whom Paul has stationed next to himself in the uninterrupted observance of abstinence: Or else, I alone and Barnabas, have not we the power of working? And, of course, the Epistle of Barnabas is more generally received among the Churches than that apocryphal Shepherd of adulterers. Warning, accordingly, the disciples to omit all first principles, and strive rather after perfection, and not lay again the foundations of repentance from the works of the dead, he says: For impossible it is that they who have once been illuminated, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have participated in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the word of God and found it sweet, when they shall — their age already setting — have fallen away, should be again recalled unto repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God, and dishonouring Him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: For there is extant withal an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas
quotes.note: Writing in early third-century Carthage, Tertullian provides the primary North African testimony attributing the Epistle to the Hebrews to Paul's apostolic companion Barnabas while quoting Hebrews 6 verbatim.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of John

quotes.quote: And the Apostle Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: At the end of the days He spoke to us in His Son, whom He made the heir of all things, 'through whom' also He made the ages, showing us that God made the ages through His Son, the through whom belonging, when the ages were being made, to the Only-begotten.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And the Apostle Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews
quotes.note: In his early third-century commentary on John, Origen cites the opening prologue of Hebrews 1:2 as the words of the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

quotes.quote: And therefore I think it sufficient to quote this one testimony of Paul from the Epistle to the Hebrews, in which he says: By faith Moses, when he had come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians.
quotes.highlight_phrase: to quote this one testimony of Paul from the Epistle to the Hebrews, in which he says
quotes.note: In the preface to his foundational theological treatise, Origen cites Hebrews 11:24–26 as an authoritative testimony of the Apostle Paul from the Epistle to the Hebrews.

quotes.quote: To show more clearly, however, what we mean, let us take the illustration employed by the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he says, For the earth, which drinks in the rain that comes oft upon it, and brings forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, will receive blessing from God; but that which bears thorns and briers is rejected, and is near unto cursing, whose end is to be burned. Now from those words of Paul which we have quoted, it is clearly shown that by one and the same act on the part of God — that, viz., by which He sends rain upon the earth — one portion of the ground, when carefully cultivated, brings forth good fruits; while another, neglected and uncared for, produces thorns and thistles.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the illustration employed by the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he says
quotes.note: Demonstrating early third-century Alexandrian usage, Origen quotes Hebrews 6:7–8 and explicitly identifies the Apostle Paul as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

works.title: Homilies on Hebrews (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: In addition he makes the following statements in regard to the Epistle to the Hebrews in his Homilies upon it: That the verbal style of the epistle entitled 'To the Hebrews,' is not rude like the language of the apostle, who acknowledged himself 'rude in speech' that is, in expression; but that its diction is purer Greek, any one who has the power to discern differences of phraseology will acknowledge. Moreover, that the thoughts of the epistle are admirable, and not inferior to the acknowledged apostolic writings, any one who carefully examines the apostolic text will admit.' Farther on he adds: If I gave my opinion, I should say that the thoughts are those of the apostle, but the diction and phraseology are those of some one who remembered the apostolic teachings, and wrote down at his leisure what had been said by his teacher. Therefore if any church holds that this epistle is by Paul, let it be commended for this. For not without reason have the ancients handed it down as Paul's. But who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows. The statement of some who have gone before us is that Clement, bishop of the Romans, wrote the epistle, and of others that Luke, the author of the Gospel and the Acts, wrote it.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Therefore if any church holds that this epistle is by Paul, let it be commended for this. For not without reason have the ancients handed it down as Paul's.
quotes.note: Origen provides the most detailed third-century philological analysis of Hebrews, affirming that ancient tradition handed it down as Paul's while recording traditions naming Luke or Clement of Rome as its scribe.

quotes.quote: For the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, in speaking of the prophets, and what they suffered, says, They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, they were slain with the sword. To whom, I ask, does the sawn asunder refer (for by an old idiom, not peculiar to Hebrew, but found also in Greek, this is said in the plural, although it refers to but one person)? Now we know very well that tradition says that Esaias the prophet was sawn asunder; and this is found in some apocryphal work, which probably the Jews have purposely tampered with, introducing some phrases manifestly incorrect, that discredit might be thrown on the whole. However, some one hard pressed by this argument may have recourse to the opinion of those who reject this Epistle as not being Paul's; against whom I must at some other time use other arguments to prove that it is Paul's.
quotes.highlight_phrase: reject this Epistle as not being Paul's; against whom I must at some other time use other arguments to prove that it is Paul's.
quotes.note: In his correspondence with Julius Africanus, Origen defends the canonical authority of Hebrews 11 and affirms that he holds distinct arguments demonstrating Pauline authorship against those who doubted it.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Thus Ignatius has done in the epistles which we have mentioned, and Clement in his epistle which is accepted by all, and which he wrote in the name of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth. In this epistle he gives many thoughts drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews, and also quotes verbally some of its expressions, thus showing most plainly that it is not a recent production. Wherefore it has seemed reasonable to reckon it with the other writings of the apostle. For as Paul had written to the Hebrews in his native tongue, some say that the evangelist Luke, others that this Clement himself, translated the epistle. The latter seems more probable, because the epistle of Clement and that to the Hebrews have a similar character in regard to style, and still further because the thoughts contained in the two works are not very different.
quotes.highlight_phrase: For as Paul had written to the Hebrews in his native tongue, some say that the evangelist Luke, others that this Clement himself, translated the epistle.
quotes.note: Eusebius cites Clement of Rome's late first-century use of Hebrews to establish its antiquity and reports the tradition that Paul composed it in Hebrew before Luke or Clement translated it.

quotes.quote: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed. It is not indeed right to overlook the fact that some have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome, on the ground that it was not written by Paul. But what has been said concerning this epistle by those who lived before our time I shall quote in the proper place. In regard to the so-called Acts of Paul, I have not found them among the undisputed writings.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed.
quotes.note: In his survey of apostolic writings, Eusebius counts Hebrews among Paul's fourteen well-known epistles while candidly recording that some in the Roman church disputed its direct Pauline authorship.

quotes.quote: But it is highly probable that the works of the ancients, which he says they had, were the Gospels and the writings of the apostles, and probably some expositions of the ancient prophets, such as are contained in the Epistle to the Hebrews, and in many others of Paul's Epistles.
quotes.highlight_phrase: such as are contained in the Epistle to the Hebrews, and in many others of Paul's Epistles
quotes.note: The fourth-century church historian Eusebius of Caesarea groups the Epistle to the Hebrews directly among the recognized Epistles of the Apostle Paul.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul.
quotes.note: In his catechetical lectures delivered in Jerusalem around AD 350, Cyril enumerates fourteen canonical Epistles of Paul, confirming the inclusion of Hebrews within the Pauline corpus.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews
quotes.note: The regional Synod of Laodicea in Asia Minor explicitly enumerates the Epistle to the Hebrews among the fourteen canonical Epistles of Paul appointed for public reading.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews
quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius of Alexandria lists the Epistle to the Hebrews among the fourteen canonical Epistles of Paul within the twenty-seven-book New Testament.

John Chrysostom.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church.
John Chrysostom.note: Patriarch of Constantinople; greatest preacher of the Greek Church. — Antioch, Syria & Constantinople

quotes.quote: The affection of Paul for him is a sufficient evidence of his character. For he elsewhere says of him, You know the proof of him, that as a son with a father, he has served with me in the Gospel. And to the Corinthians again he writes: I have sent unto you Timothy, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord. And again: Let no man despise him, for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. And to the Hebrews he writes, Know that our brother Timothy is set at liberty. Indeed his love for him is everywhere apparent, and the miracles that are now wrought still attest his claims. 2. If it should be asked why he addresses Epistles to Titus and Timothy alone, though Silas was approved, as also was Luke, for he writes, Only Luke is with me, and Clement was one of his associates, of whom he says, with Clement and other my fellow-laborers, for what reason then does he write only to Titus and Timothy? It is because he had already committed the care of churches to these, and certain marked places had been assigned to them, but the others were in attendance upon him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And to the Hebrews he writes, Know that our brother Timothy is set at liberty.
quotes.note: In his introduction to First Timothy, John Chrysostom cites Hebrews 13:23 as Paul's own testimony regarding his close companion Timothy.

quotes.quote: The blessed Paul, writing to the Romans, says, "Inasmuch then as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office: if by any means I may provoke to emulation them that are my flesh": and again, in another place, "For He that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles." If therefore he were the Apostle of the Gentiles, (for also in the Acts, God said to him, "Depart; for I will send you far hence unto the Gentiles," what had he to do with the Hebrews? And why did he also write an Epistle to them?
quotes.highlight_phrase: what had he to do with the Hebrews? And why did he also write an Epistle to them?
quotes.note: Introducing his homilies on Hebrews in Antioch, John Chrysostom affirms Pauline authorship and addresses why the Apostle to the Gentiles also composed an epistle for Jewish believers.

quotes.quote: God who at sundry times and in various manners spoke in time past unto the fathers by the Prophets, has at the end of the days spoken unto us by His Son whom He has appointed heir of all things, by whom also He made the worlds. 1. Truly, where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. This at least the blessed Paul intimates here also, in the very beginning of his Epistle to the Hebrews. For since as it was likely that afflicted, worn out by evils, and judging of things thereby, they would think themselves worse off than all other men, — he shows that herein they had rather been made partakers of greater, even very exceeding, grace; arousing the hearer at the very opening of his discourse. Wherefore he says, God who at sundry times and in various manners spoke in times past unto the fathers by the Prophets, has at the end of the days spoken unto us by His Son.
quotes.highlight_phrase: This at least the blessed Paul intimates here also, in the very beginning of his Epistle to the Hebrews.
quotes.note: Opening his homilies on the epistle in Antioch and Constantinople, John Chrysostom explicitly identifies the blessed Paul as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

quotes.quote: Moses having written five books, has nowhere put his own name to them, neither have they who after him put together the history of events after him, no nor yet has Matthew, nor John, nor Mark, nor Luke; but the blessed Paul everywhere in his Epistles sets his own name. Now why was this? Because they were writing to people, who were present, and it had been superfluous to show themselves when they were present. But this man sent his writings from afar and in the form of a letter, for which cause also the addition of the name was necessary. But if in the Epistle to the Hebrews he does not do the same, this too is after his own wise judgment. For since they felt prejudiced against him, lest on hearing the name at the outstart, they should stop up all admission to his discourse, he subtly won their attention by concealing the name.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But if in the Epistle to the Hebrews he does not do the same, this too is after his own wise judgment.
quotes.note: Contrasting the anonymous Gospels with Paul's signed letters, John Chrysostom explains that Paul intentionally omitted his name from the opening of Hebrews to avoid alienating prejudiced Jewish readers.

quotes.quote: In thus saluting all through the Epistle addressed to the Corinthians, he would at once honor these, and bring together the whole nation. But he calls them saints, thereby implying that if any be an impure person, he has no share in this salutation. But why, writing to the mother city, does he address all through her, since he does not so everywhere? For instance, in his Epistle to the Thessalonians he addressed not the Macedonians also; and in like manner in that to the Ephesians he does not include all Asia; neither was that to the Romans written to those also who dwell in Italy. But in this Epistle he does so; and in that to the Galatians. For there also he writes not to one city, or two, or three, but to all who are scattered every where, saying, Paul an Apostle, (not from men neither through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, Who raised Him from the dead,) and all the brethren which are with me, unto the Churches of Galatia. Grace to you and peace. To the Hebrews also he writes one Epistle to all collectively; not distinguishing them into their several cities. What then can be the reason of this? Because, as I think, in this case all were involved in one common disorder, wherefore also he addresses them in common, as needing one common remedy. For the Galatians were all of them infected. So too were the Hebrews, and so I think these (Achaians) also.
quotes.highlight_phrase: To the Hebrews also he writes one Epistle to all collectively; not distinguishing them into their several cities.
quotes.note: Comparing Paul's epistolary salutations across the New Testament, John Chrysostom explains that Paul addressed the Epistle to the Hebrews collectively to the entire Jewish Christian community rather than to a single city.

works.title: Homilies on the Gospel of John (Homily 2)

quotes.quote: And that you may not suffer this, (I shall not cease continually thus to warn you,) strengthen your minds, that you may not hear what the faithful among the Hebrews heard from Paul. For to them he said that he had many things to say, and hard to be uttered; not as though they were by nature such, but because, says he, you are dull of hearing.
quotes.highlight_phrase: that you may not hear what the faithful among the Hebrews heard from Paul
quotes.note: Preaching on the Gospel of John, Chrysostom cites Hebrews 5:11 as the admonition delivered to the faithful among the Hebrews by the Apostle Paul.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: He then, in the fourteenth year of Nero on the same day with Peter, was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake and was buried in the Ostian way, the twenty-seventh year after our Lord's passion. He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: To the Romans one, To the Corinthians two, To the Galatians one, To the Ephesians one, To the Philippians one, To the Colossians one, To the Thessalonians two; and besides these to his disciples, To Timothy two, To Titus one, To Philemon one. The epistle which is called the Epistle to the Hebrews is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language, but it is reckoned, either according to Tertullian to be the work of Barnabas, or according to others, to be by Luke the Evangelist or Clement afterwards bishop of the church at Rome, who, they say, arranged and adorned the ideas of Paul in his own language, though to be sure, since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account. He being a Hebrew wrote Hebrew, that is his own tongue and most fluently while the things which were eloquently written in Hebrew were more eloquently turned into Greek and this is the reason why it seems to differ from other epistles of Paul. Some read one also to the Laodiceans but it is rejected by everyone.
quotes.highlight_phrase: since Paul was writing to Hebrews and was in disrepute among them he may have omitted his name from the salutation on this account
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of Christian writers, Jerome surveys the early traditions attributing Hebrews' Greek text to Barnabas, Luke, or Clement while explaining that Paul originally composed it in Hebrew.

quotes.quote: Clement, of whom the apostle Paul writing to the Philippians says With Clement and others of my fellow-workers whose names are written in the book of life, the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter, if indeed the second was Linus and the third Anacletus, although most of the Latins think that Clement was second after the apostle. He wrote, on the part of the church of Rome, an especially valuable Letter to the church of the Corinthians, which in some places is publicly read, and which seems to me to agree in style with the epistle to the Hebrews which passes under the name of Paul but it differs from this same epistle, not only in many of its ideas, but also in respect of the order of words, and its likeness in either respect is not very great.
quotes.highlight_phrase: agree in style with the epistle to the Hebrews which passes under the name of Paul
quotes.note: Evaluating the biography of Clement of Rome, Jerome compares the literary style of First Clement with the Epistle to the Hebrews, which circulated under the name of Paul.

quotes.quote: Gaius, bishop of Rome, in the time of Zephyrinus, that is, in the reign of Antoninus, the son of Severus, delivered a very notable disputation Against Proculus, the follower of Montanus, convicting him of temerity in his defense of the new prophecy, and in the same volume also enumerating only thirteen epistles of Paul, says that the fourteenth, which is now called, To the Hebrews, is not by him, and is not considered among the Romans to the present day as being by the apostle Paul.
quotes.highlight_phrase: enumerating only thirteen epistles of Paul, says that the fourteenth, which is now called, To the Hebrews, is not by him
quotes.note: Jerome records that the early third-century Roman writer Gaius counted thirteen Pauline letters, reflecting the longstanding reluctance among some Latin churches to attribute the fourteenth epistle, Hebrews, directly to Paul.

quotes.quote: The apostle Paul writes to seven churches (for the eighth epistle — that to the Hebrews — is not generally counted in with the others). He instructs Timothy and Titus; he intercedes with Philemon for his runaway slave. Of him I think it better to say nothing than to write inadequately.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The apostle Paul writes to seven churches (for the eighth epistle — that to the Hebrews — is not generally counted in with the others).
quotes.note: In his survey of biblical books addressed to Paulinus of Nola, Jerome summarizes Paul's church epistles while noting that the Epistle to the Hebrews was often set apart from the seven-church collection.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews
quotes.note: In his treatise on biblical interpretation, Augustine of Hippo explicitly lists the Epistle to the Hebrews among the fourteen canonical epistles of the Apostle Paul.

Council of Carthage.apostolic_link: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine.
Council of Carthage.note: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Canons of the Council of Carthage

quotes.quote: Item, that besides the Canonical Scriptures nothing be read in church under the name of divine Scripture. But the Canonical Scriptures are as follows: Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy. Joshua the Son of Nun. The Judges. Ruth. The Kings, iv. books. The Chronicles, ij. books. Job. The Psalter. The Five books of Solomon. The Twelve Books of the Prophets. Isaiah. Jeremiah. Ezechiel. Daniel. Tobit. Judith. Esther. Ezra, ij. books. Macchabees, ij. books. The New Testament. The Gospels, iv. books. The Acts of the Apostles, j. book. The Epistles of Paul, xiv. The Epistles of Peter, the Apostle, ij. The Epistles of John the Apostle, iij. The Epistles of James the Apostle, j. The Epistle of Jude the Apostle, j. The Revelation of John, j. book. Let this be sent to our brother and fellow bishop, Boniface, and to the other bishops of those parts, that they may confirm this canon, for these are the things which we have received from our fathers to be read in church.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The Epistles of Paul, xiv.
quotes.note: The North African bishops at the Council of Carthage formally ratified the twenty-seven-book New Testament canon, counting fourteen Epistles of Paul to include the Epistle to the Hebrews.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul
quotes.note: In his exposition of the creed for the church at Aquileia, Rufinus enumerates fourteen canonical Epistles of the Apostle Paul, attesting to northern Italian reception of Hebrews within the Pauline corpus.

quotes.quote: I Believe, therefore, is placed in the forefront, as the Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says, He that comes to God must first of all believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who believe in Him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: as the Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy, Rufinus of Aquileia cites Hebrews 11:6 and explicitly attributes the Epistle to the Hebrews to the Apostle Paul.

book_meta.author_role: Brother of the Lord & Bishop of the Jerusalem Church
book_meta.earliest_manuscripts: 𝔓20 (3rd cent.), 𝔓23 (c. AD 200–250), Codex Sinaiticus & Vaticanus

internal_evidence.summary: Opens with 'James, a bondservant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes who are dispersed abroad', saturated with Jesus's Sermon on the Mount.

verse_details.text: James, a bond-servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes who are dispersed abroad: Greetings.
My brethren, do not hold your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with [an attitude of] personal favoritism.
Therefore be patient, brethren, until the coming of the Lord. The farmer waits for the precious produce of the soil, being patient about it, until it gets the early and late rains.
You too be patient; strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Critics point out that James was listed among the Antilegomena (disputed/scrutinized) by Eusebius in the early 4th century.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Eusebius notes that while some scrutinized it, it was publicly read in the vast majority of churches; Origen cites James explicitly as Scripture in his Commentary on John and Commentary on Romans, and Athanasius and Jerome confirm its apostolic authority.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: These things are recorded in regard to James, who is said to be the author of the first of the so-called catholic epistles. But it is to be observed that it is disputed; at least, not many of the ancients have mentioned it, as is the case likewise with the epistle that bears the name of Jude, which is also one of the seven so-called catholic epistles. Nevertheless we know that these also, with the rest, have been read publicly in very many churches.
quotes.highlight_phrase: James, who is said to be the author of the first of the so-called catholic epistles.
quotes.note: Concluding his historical account of the martyrdom of James the Just, Eusebius notes that the first of the Catholic Epistles attributed to James was read publicly across numerous churches despite early debate.

quotes.quote: Since we are dealing with this subject it is proper to sum up the writings of the New Testament which have been already mentioned. First then must be put the holy quaternion of the Gospels; following them the Acts of the Apostles. After this must be reckoned the epistles of Paul; next in order the extant former epistle of John, and likewise the epistle of Peter, must be maintained. After them is to be placed, if it really seem proper, the Apocalypse of John, concerning which we shall give the different opinions at the proper time. These then belong among the accepted writings. Among the disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many, are extant the so-called epistle of James and that of Jude, also the second epistle of Peter, and those that are called the second and third of John, whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Among the disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many, are extant the so-called epistle of James
quotes.note: In his foundational fourth-century survey of the New Testament canon, the church historian Eusebius records that the Epistle of James, though disputed by some, was widely recognized across the churches.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude
quotes.note: Instructing catechumens in Jerusalem around AD 350, Bishop Cyril enumerates the authoritative New Testament canon and places the Epistle of James at the head of the seven Catholic Epistles.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude
quotes.note: The regional Synod of Laodicea in Asia Minor formally lists one epistle of James first among the seven canonical Catholic Epistles appointed for liturgical reading in the churches.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude.
