quotes.note: In his landmark Easter letter of AD 367, Athanasius of Alexandria defines the twenty-seven-book New Testament canon and affirms one epistle of James among the seven Catholic Epistles.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: James, who is called the brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, the son of Joseph by another wife, as some think, but, as appears to me, the son of Mary sister of the mother of our Lord of whom John makes mention in his book, after our Lord's passion at once ordained by the apostles bishop of Jerusalem, wrote a single epistle, which is reckoned among the seven Catholic Epistles and even this is claimed by some to have been published by some one else under his name, and gradually, as time went on, to have gained authority.
quotes.highlight_phrase: ordained by the apostles bishop of Jerusalem, wrote a single epistle, which is reckoned among the seven Catholic Epistles
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of Christian writers, Jerome identifies James the Just, the first bishop of Jerusalem, as the author of a single letter among the seven Catholic Epistles.

quotes.quote: The apostles James, Peter, John, and Jude, have published seven epistles at once spiritual and to the point, short and long, short that is in words but lengthy in substance so that there are few indeed who do not find themselves in the dark when they read them. The apocalypse of John has as many mysteries as words. In saying this I have said less than the book deserves. All praise of it is inadequate; manifold meanings lie hidden in its every word.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The apostles James, Peter, John, and Jude, have published seven epistles
quotes.note: Writing to Paulinus of Nola across the books of Scripture, Jerome groups James with Peter, John, and Jude as the apostolic authors of the seven canonical Catholic Epistles.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James;
quotes.note: In his treatise on biblical interpretation, Augustine of Hippo enumerates the authoritative New Testament books received across the churches and includes one epistle by James.

Council of Carthage.apostolic_link: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine.
Council of Carthage.note: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Canons of the Council of Carthage

quotes.quote: Item, that besides the Canonical Scriptures nothing be read in church under the name of divine Scripture. But the Canonical Scriptures are as follows: Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy. Joshua the Son of Nun. The Judges. Ruth. The Kings, iv. books. The Chronicles, ij. books. Job. The Psalter. The Five books of Solomon. The Twelve Books of the Prophets. Isaiah. Jeremiah. Ezechiel. Daniel. Tobit. Judith. Esther. Ezra, ij. books. Macchabees, ij. books. The New Testament. The Gospels, iv. books. The Acts of the Apostles, j. book. The Epistles of Paul, xiv. The Epistles of Peter, the Apostle, ij. The Epistles of John the Apostle, iij. The Epistles of James the Apostle, j. The Epistle of Jude the Apostle, j. The Revelation of John, j. book. Let this be sent to our brother and fellow bishop, Boniface, and to the other bishops of those parts, that they may confirm this canon, for these are the things which we have received from our fathers to be read in church.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The Epistles of James the Apostle, j.
quotes.note: The North African Council of Carthage formally ratifies the liturgical canon of Scripture and includes one epistle of James the Apostle among the received books of the New Testament.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle,
quotes.note: In his Latin exposition of the creed, Rufinus of Aquileia catalogs the received New Testament canon and explicitly attributes the Epistle of James to James, the brother of the Lord.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle of Jesus Christ & Eyewitness of His Sufferings

internal_evidence.summary: Peter identifies himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ and fellow elder who witnessed Christ's sufferings, writing through Silvanus from 'Babylon' (Rome) with his son Mark.

verse_details.text: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who reside as aliens, scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, who are chosen
Therefore, I exhort the elders among you, as [your] fellow elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker also of the glory that is to be revealed,
Through Silvanus, our faithful brother (for so I regard [him]), I have written to you briefly, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it!
She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, and [so does] my son, Mark.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Some modern critics argue the Greek is too refined for a Galilean fisherman.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Peter explicitly states he wrote through Silvanus (Silas, a Roman citizen and prophet; 1 Pet 5:12) as amanuensis; 1 Peter is universally acknowledged as authentic in antiquity, cited by Polycarp, Papias, Irenaeus, Clement, Tertullian, and Origen.

Papias of Hierapolis.apostolic_link: Hearer of the Apostle John and the Presbyter John; companion of Polycarp.
Papias of Hierapolis.note: Hearer of the Apostle John and the Presbyter John; companion of Polycarp. — Hierapolis, Asia Minor

works.title: Expositions of Oracles of the Lord (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: But concerning Matthew he writes as follows: So then Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able. And the same writer uses testimonies from the first Epistle of John and from that of Peter likewise.
quotes.highlight_phrase: uses testimonies from the first Epistle of John and from that of Peter likewise.
quotes.note: Preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea, this testimony from Papias of Hierapolis confirms that First Peter was already cited as an authoritative apostolic writing in early second-century Asia Minor.

quotes.quote: [This is what is related by Papias regarding Mark; but with regard to Matthew he has made the following statements]: Matthew put together the oracles [of the Lord] in the Hebrew language, and each one interpreted them as best he could. [The same person uses proofs from the First Epistle of John, and from the Epistle of Peter in like manner. And he also gives another story of a woman who was accused of many sins before the Lord, which is to be found in the Gospel according to the Hebrews.]
quotes.highlight_phrase: uses proofs from the First Epistle of John, and from the Epistle of Peter in like manner.
quotes.note: Papias of Hierapolis, an early second-century hearer of the Apostle John, provides the earliest recorded external attestation to the authoritative use of First Peter alongside First John.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: As, therefore, when that which is perfect has come, we shall not see another Father, but Him whom we now desire to see (for blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God ); neither shall we look for another Christ and Son of God, but Him who [was born] of the Virgin Mary, who also suffered, in whom too we trust, and whom we love; as Esaias says: And they shall say in that day, Behold our Lord God, in whom we have trusted, and we have rejoiced in our salvation; and Peter says in his Epistle: Whom, not seeing, you love; in whom, though now you see Him not, you have believed, you shall rejoice with joy unspeakable; neither do we receive another Holy Spirit, besides Him who is with us, and who cries, Abba, Father; and we shall make increase in the very same things [as now], and shall make progress, so that no longer through a glass, or by means of enigmas, but face to face, we shall enjoy the gifts of God — so also now, receiving more than the temple, and more than Solomon, that is, the advent of the Son of God, we have not been taught another God besides the Framer and the Maker of all, who has been pointed out to us from the beginning; nor another Christ, the Son of God, besides Him who was foretold by the prophets.
quotes.highlight_phrase: and Peter says in his Epistle: Whom, not seeing, you love; in whom, though now you see Him not, you have believed
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul around 180 AD, Irenaeus of Lyons quotes First Peter 1:8 directly as the words of the Apostle Peter in his Epistle alongside Isaiah and the Gospels.

Clement of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen.
Clement of Alexandria.note: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: And one aim and one end, as far as regards perfection, being demonstrated to belong to the man and the woman, Peter in his Epistle says, Though now for a season, if need be, you are in heaviness through manifold temptations; that the trial of your faith, being much more precious than that of gold which perishes, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise, and honour, and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ; whom, having not seen, you love; in whom, though now you see Him not, yet believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable, and full of glory, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Peter in his Epistle says, Though now for a season, if need be, you are in heaviness through manifold temptations
quotes.note: Head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria in the late second century, Clement quotes First Peter 1:6–9 verbatim and attributes the epistle directly to the Apostle Peter.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: Addressing the Christians of Pontus, Peter, at all events, says, How great indeed is the glory, if you suffer patiently, without being punished as evildoers! For this is a lovely feature, and even hereunto were you called, since Christ also suffered for us, leaving you Himself as an example, that you should follow His own steps.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Addressing the Christians of Pontus, Peter, at all events, says, How great indeed is the glory, if you suffer patiently
quotes.note: Writing from Carthage in the early third century, Tertullian explicitly cites First Peter 2:20–21 as the Apostle Peter's own letter addressed to the Christians of Pontus.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

works.title: Commentary on Matthew (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: In his first book on Matthew's Gospel, maintaining the Canon of the Church, he testifies that he knows only four Gospels, writing as follows: Among the four Gospels, which are the only indisputable ones in the Church of God under heaven, I have learned by tradition that the first was written by Matthew, who was once a publican, but afterwards an apostle of Jesus Christ, and it was prepared for the converts from Judaism, and published in the Hebrew language. The second is by Mark, who composed it according to the instructions of Peter, who in his Catholic epistle acknowledges him as a son, saying, 'The church that is at Babylon elected together with you, salutes you, and so does Marcus, my son.' And the third by Luke, the Gospel commended by Paul, and composed for Gentile converts. Last of all that by John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Peter, who in his Catholic epistle acknowledges him as a son, saying, 'The church that is at Babylon elected together with you, salutes you, and so does Marcus, my son.'
quotes.note: In his defense of the ecclesiastical canon, Origen of Alexandria explicitly cites First Peter 5:13 as Peter's own Catholic Epistle confirming his close relationship with Mark.

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of John

quotes.quote: As to the descent into Hades, we read in the sixteenth Psalm, You will not leave my soul in Hades, and as for the journey in prison with the Spirit we read in Peter in his Catholic Epistle, Put to death, he says, in the flesh, but quickened in the Spirit; in which also He went and preached unto the spirits in prison, which at one time were disobedient, when the long-suffering of God once waited in the days of Noah while the ark was a preparing.
quotes.highlight_phrase: we read in Peter in his Catholic Epistle, Put to death, he says, in the flesh, but quickened in the Spirit
quotes.note: In his Greek commentary on the Gospel of John, Origen of Alexandria cites First Peter 3:18–20 alongside the Psalms as Peter's authoritative Catholic Epistle.

quotes.quote: They do not read what is written respecting the hope of those who were destroyed in the deluge; of which hope Peter himself thus speaks in his first Epistle: That Christ, indeed, was put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit, by which He went and preached to the spirits who were kept in prison, who once were unbelievers, when they awaited the long-suffering of God in the days of Noah, when the ark was preparing, in which a few, i.e., eight souls, were saved by water. Whereunto also baptism by a like figure now saves you.
quotes.highlight_phrase: of which hope Peter himself thus speaks in his first Epistle: That Christ, indeed, was put to death in the flesh
quotes.note: In his foundational treatise on Christian theology, Origen of Alexandria quotes First Peter 3:18–21 and explicitly attributes the passage to Peter speaking in his First Epistle.

works.title: Expositions of John's Gospel (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: In the fifth book of his Expositions of John's Gospel, he speaks thus concerning the epistles of the apostles: But he who was 'made sufficient to be a minister of the New Testament, not of the letter, but of the Spirit,' that is, Paul, who 'fully preached the Gospel from Jerusalem and round about even unto Illyricum,' did not write to all the churches which he had instructed and to those to which he wrote he sent but few lines. And Peter, on whom the Church of Christ is built, 'against which the gates of hell shall not prevail,' has left one acknowledged epistle; perhaps also a second, but this is doubtful. Why need we speak of him who reclined upon the bosom of Jesus, John, who has left us one Gospel, though he confessed that he might write so many that the world could not contain them? And he wrote also the Apocalypse, but was commanded to keep silence and not to write the words of the seven thunders. He has left also an epistle of very few lines; perhaps also a second and third; but not all consider them genuine, and together they do not contain hundred lines.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And Peter, on whom the Church of Christ is built, 'against which the gates of hell shall not prevail,' has left one acknowledged epistle
quotes.note: Origen of Alexandria surveys the New Testament writings in the early third century and testifies that Peter's First Epistle was universally acknowledged across the church.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: Therefore, beloved brethren, we must be on our guard, and strive with all our powers to repel, with solicitous and full watch-fullness, the enemy, raging and aiming his darts against every part of our body in which we can be stricken and wounded, in accordance with what the Apostle Peter, in his epistle, forewarns and teaches, saying, Be sober, and watch; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about seeking any one to devour.
quotes.highlight_phrase: what the Apostle Peter, in his epistle, forewarns and teaches, saying
quotes.note: In his pastoral treatise on envy, Cyprian of Carthage invokes 1 Peter 5:8 as the direct apostolic admonition of Peter to the universal Church.

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: In the Epistle of Peter to them of Pontus: Nor let any of you suffer as a thief, or a murderer, or as an evil-doer, or as a minder of other people's business, but as a Christian.
quotes.highlight_phrase: In the Epistle of Peter to them of Pontus
quotes.note: Writing from third-century North Africa, Cyprian of Carthage explicitly attributes 1 Peter 4:15–16 to the Apostle Peter and identifies the letter by its opening address to the believers in Pontus.

quotes.quote: Of this same thing in the Epistle of Peter to the people at Pontus: Let there be in a woman not the outward adorning of ornament, or of gold, or of apparel, but the adorning of the heart.
quotes.highlight_phrase: in the Epistle of Peter to the people at Pontus
quotes.note: Cyprian of Carthage cites 1 Peter 3:3–4 as the authoritative teaching of the Apostle Peter, designating the epistle by its first named recipients in Pontus.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: 1. One epistle of Peter, that called the first, is acknowledged as genuine. And this the ancient elders used freely in their own writings as an undisputed work. But we have learned that his extant second Epistle does not belong to the canon; yet, as it has appeared profitable to many, it has been used with the other Scriptures. 2. The so-called Acts of Peter, however, and the Gospel which bears his name, and the Preaching and the Apocalypse, as they are called, we know have not been universally accepted, because no ecclesiastical writer, ancient or modern, has made use of testimonies drawn from them. 3. But in the course of my history I shall be careful to show, in addition to the official succession, what ecclesiastical writers have from time to time made use of any of the disputed works, and what they have said in regard to the canonical and accepted writings, as well as in regard to those which are not of this class. 4. Such are the writings that bear the name of Peter, only one of which I know to be genuine and acknowledged by the ancient elders.
quotes.highlight_phrase: One epistle of Peter, that called the first, is acknowledged as genuine. And this the ancient elders used freely in their own writings as an undisputed work.
quotes.note: Having access to the ecclesiastical library at Caesarea, Eusebius testifies that First Peter was universally acknowledged as authentic and cited without dispute by the earliest generations of Christian elders.

quotes.quote: And so greatly did the splendor of piety illumine the minds of Peter's hearers that they were not satisfied with hearing once only, and were not content with the unwritten teaching of the divine Gospel, but with all sorts of entreaties they besought Mark, a follower of Peter, and the one whose Gospel is extant, that he would leave them a written monument of the doctrine which had been orally communicated to them. Nor did they cease until they had prevailed with the man, and had thus become the occasion of the written Gospel which bears the name of Mark. And they say that Peter — when he had learned, through a revelation of the Spirit, of that which had been done — was pleased with the zeal of the men, and that the work obtained the sanction of his authority for the purpose of being used in the churches. Clement in the eighth book of his Hypotyposes gives this account, and with him agrees the bishop of Hierapolis named Papias. And Peter makes mention of Mark in his first epistle which they say that he wrote in Rome itself, as is indicated by him, when he calls the city, by a figure, Babylon, as he does in the following words: The church that is at Babylon, elected together with you, salutes you; and so does Marcus my son.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And Peter makes mention of Mark in his first epistle which they say that he wrote in Rome itself, as is indicated by him, when he calls the city, by a figure, Babylon
quotes.note: Drawing on Clement of Alexandria and Papias, Eusebius records the ancient tradition that Peter composed his First Epistle from Rome, figuratively referred to as Babylon, alongside his disciple Mark.

quotes.quote: And in how many provinces Peter preached Christ and taught the doctrine of the new covenant to those of the circumcision is clear from his own words in his epistle already mentioned as undisputed, in which he writes to the Hebrews of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.
quotes.highlight_phrase: is clear from his own words in his epistle already mentioned as undisputed, in which he writes to the Hebrews of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.
quotes.note: Eusebius cites the opening prescript of First Peter 1:1 as Peter's own undisputed testimony regarding his missionary jurisdiction among the scattered believers of Asia Minor.

quotes.quote: Since we are dealing with this subject it is proper to sum up the writings of the New Testament which have been already mentioned. First then must be put the holy quaternion of the Gospels; following them the Acts of the Apostles. After this must be reckoned the epistles of Paul; next in order the extant former epistle of John, and likewise the epistle of Peter, must be maintained. After them is to be placed, if it really seem proper, the Apocalypse of John, concerning which we shall give the different opinions at the proper time. These then belong among the accepted writings. Among the disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many, are extant the so-called epistle of James and that of Jude, also the second epistle of Peter, and those that are called the second and third of John, whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name.
quotes.highlight_phrase: next in order the extant former epistle of John, and likewise the epistle of Peter, must be maintained.
quotes.note: In his landmark fourth-century classification of the New Testament writings, Eusebius places First Peter in the highest tier of universally accepted books alongside the four Gospels, Acts, and Paul's Epistles.

quotes.quote: But Polycarp, in his above-mentioned epistle to the Philippians, which is still extant, has made use of certain testimonies drawn from the First Epistle of Peter.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Polycarp, in his above-mentioned epistle to the Philippians, which is still extant, has made use of certain testimonies drawn from the First Epistle of Peter.
quotes.note: Eusebius highlights that Polycarp of Smyrna, a direct disciple of the apostles, repeatedly wove quotations from First Peter into his early second-century Epistle to the Philippians.

quotes.quote: He states these things concerning the Apocalypse in the work referred to. He also mentions the first Epistle of John, taking many proofs from it, and likewise the first Epistle of Peter.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He also mentions the first Epistle of John, taking many proofs from it, and likewise the first Epistle of Peter.
quotes.note: Summarizing the second-century writings of Irenaeus of Lyons, Eusebius records that Irenaeus repeatedly drew authoritative scriptural proofs from the First Epistle of Peter.

Cyril of Jerusalem.apostolic_link: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures.
Cyril of Jerusalem.note: Bishop of Jerusalem; delivered the famous Catechetical Lectures. — Jerusalem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Then of the New Testament there are the four Gospels only, for the rest have false titles and are mischievous. The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas, which being tinctured with the fragrance of the evangelic title corrupts the souls of the simple sort. Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; and as a seal upon them all, and the last work of the disciples, the fourteen Epistles of Paul. But let all the rest be put aside in a secondary rank. And whatever books are not read in Churches, these read not even by yourself, as you have heard me say.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Receive also the Acts of the Twelve Apostles; and in addition to these the seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude
quotes.note: Writing in mid-fourth-century Jerusalem, Bishop Cyril instructs catechumens to receive the seven Catholic Epistles—including the two Epistles of Peter—as authoritative New Testament Scripture read publicly in the churches.

Synod of Laodicea.apostolic_link: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading.
Synod of Laodicea.note: Regional synod of Asia Minor bishops regulating ecclesiastical reading. — Laodicea, Asia Minor

works.title: Canons of the Synod of Laodicea

quotes.quote: And these are the books of the New Testament: Four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; The Acts of the Apostles; Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude; Fourteen Epistles of Paul, one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Seven Catholic Epistles, to wit, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude
quotes.note: The fourth-century Synod of Laodicea in Phrygia formally catalogs the canonical books appointed for public reading across the churches of Asia Minor, including both Epistles of Peter.

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude.
quotes.note: In his 367 AD Paschal encyclical, Athanasius of Alexandria enumerates the twenty-seven books of the New Testament canon, listing both Epistles of Peter among the seven Catholic Epistles.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Simon Peter the son of John, from the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, brother of Andrew the apostle, and himself chief of the apostles, after having been bishop of the church of Antioch and having preached to the Dispersion — the believers in circumcision, in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia — pushed on to Rome in the second year of Claudius to overthrow Simon Magus, and held the sacerdotal chair there for twenty-five years until the last, that is the fourteenth, year of Nero. At his hands he received the crown of martyrdom being nailed to the cross with his head towards the ground and his feet raised on high, asserting that he was unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord. He wrote two epistles which are called Catholic, the second of which, on account of its difference from the first in style, is considered by many not to be by him. Then too the Gospel according to Mark, who was his disciple and interpreter, is ascribed to him. On the other hand, the books, of which one is entitled his Acts, another his Gospel, a third his Preaching, a fourth his Revelation, a fifth his Judgment are rejected as apocryphal.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote two epistles which are called Catholic, the second of which, on account of its difference from the first in style, is considered by many not to be by him.
quotes.note: In the opening biography of his patristic catalog, Jerome summarizes Peter's ministry across Asia Minor and Rome and affirms the undisputed Petrine authorship of the First Catholic Epistle.

quotes.quote: Mark the disciple and interpreter of Peter wrote a short gospel at the request of the brethren at Rome embodying what he had heard Peter tell. When Peter had heard this, he approved it and published it to the churches to be read by his authority as Clemens in the sixth book of his Hypotyposes and Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, record. Peter also mentions this Mark in his first epistle, figuratively indicating Rome under the name of Babylon She who is in Babylon elect together with you salutes you and so does Mark my son. So, taking the gospel which he himself composed, he went to Egypt and first preaching Christ at Alexandria he formed a church so admirable in doctrine and continence of living that he constrained all followers of Christ to his example.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Peter also mentions this Mark in his first epistle, figuratively indicating Rome under the name of Babylon
quotes.note: In his biographical entry on Mark the Evangelist, Jerome cites First Peter 5:13 as historical evidence that Peter composed his First Epistle from Rome alongside Mark.

quotes.quote: The apostles James, Peter, John, and Jude, have published seven epistles at once spiritual and to the point, short and long, short that is in words but lengthy in substance so that there are few indeed who do not find themselves in the dark when they read them. The apocalypse of John has as many mysteries as words. In saying this I have said less than the book deserves. All praise of it is inadequate; manifold meanings lie hidden in its every word.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The apostles James, Peter, John, and Jude, have published seven epistles at once spiritual and to the point
quotes.note: In his treatise on the study of Scripture addressed to Paulinus of Nola, Jerome attests to the apostolic authorship and theological depth of the Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James
quotes.note: Augustine of Hippo sets forth the complete twenty-seven-book New Testament canon recognized across the Western churches, enumerating the two Epistles of Peter among the apostolic letters.

Council of Carthage.apostolic_link: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine.
Council of Carthage.note: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Canons of the Council of Carthage

quotes.quote: Item, that besides the Canonical Scriptures nothing be read in church under the name of divine Scripture. But the Canonical Scriptures are as follows: Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy. Joshua the Son of Nun. The Judges. Ruth. The Kings, iv. books. The Chronicles, ij. books. Job. The Psalter. The Five books of Solomon. The Twelve Books of the Prophets. Isaiah. Jeremiah. Ezechiel. Daniel. Tobit. Judith. Esther. Ezra, ij. books. Macchabees, ij. books. The New Testament. The Gospels, iv. books. The Acts of the Apostles, j. book. The Epistles of Paul, xiv. The Epistles of Peter, the Apostle, ij. The Epistles of John the Apostle, iij. The Epistles of James the Apostle, j. The Epistle of Jude the Apostle, j. The Revelation of John, j. book. Let this be sent to our brother and fellow bishop, Boniface, and to the other bishops of those parts, that they may confirm this canon, for these are the things which we have received from our fathers to be read in church.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The Epistles of Peter, the Apostle, ij.
quotes.note: The North African bishops assembled at the Council of Carthage formally ratify the liturgical canon of Scripture received from their fathers, explicitly including the two Epistles of the Apostle Peter.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the close of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records the traditional New Testament canon handed down by the Fathers, including two Epistles of the Apostle Peter.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle of Jesus Christ facing imminent death

internal_evidence.summary: Simon Peter testifies as an eyewitness of the Transfiguration on the holy mountain (2 Pet 1:16–18), recalls Jesus predicting his death (2 Pet 1:14), and refers to Paul's letters as Scripture (2 Pet 3:15–16).

verse_details.text: Simon Peter, a bond-servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have received a faith of the same kind as ours, by the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ:
knowing that the laying aside of my [earthly] dwelling is imminent, as also our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me.
For we did not follow cleverly devised tales when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty.
For when He received honor and glory from God the Father, such an utterance as this was made to Him by the Majestic Glory, "This is My beloved Son with whom I am well-pleased "--
and we ourselves heard this utterance made from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.
and regard the patience of our Lord [as] salvation; just as also our beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you,

as also in all [his] letters, speaking in them of these things, in which are some things hard to understand, which the untaught and unstable distort, as [they do] also the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: 2 Peter was the most disputed book in the early canon due to stylistic divergence from 1 Peter and overlap with Jude.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Jerome explains that Peter employed different amanuenses for the two letters; the Transfiguration testimony and high view of Paul's letters reflect a 1st-century eyewitness; preserved in 𝔓72 and canonized at Carthage (AD 397).

Athanasius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy.
Athanasius of Alexandria.note: Patriarch of Alexandria; champion of Nicene orthodoxy. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: Again it is not tedious to speak of the [books] of the New Testament. These are, the four Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles and Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians; next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John. 6. These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Epistles (called Catholic ), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three; after these, one of Jude.
quotes.note: In his landmark AD 367 paschal letter to the Egyptian churches, Athanasius of Alexandria formally ratifies two epistles of Peter within the twenty-seven-book New Testament canon.

Jerome.apostolic_link: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate.
Jerome.note: Foremost biblical scholar and linguist of the Latin Church; translator of the Vulgate. — Rome, Italy & Bethlehem, Palestine

quotes.quote: Simon Peter the son of John, from the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, brother of Andrew the apostle, and himself chief of the apostles, after having been bishop of the church of Antioch and having preached to the Dispersion — the believers in circumcision, in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia — pushed on to Rome in the second year of Claudius to overthrow Simon Magus, and held the sacerdotal chair there for twenty-five years until the last, that is the fourteenth, year of Nero. At his hands he received the crown of martyrdom being nailed to the cross with his head towards the ground and his feet raised on high, asserting that he was unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord. He wrote two epistles which are called Catholic, the second of which, on account of its difference from the first in style, is considered by many not to be by him. Then too the Gospel according to Mark, who was his disciple and interpreter, is ascribed to him. On the other hand, the books, of which one is entitled his Acts, another his Gospel, a third his Preaching, a fourth his Revelation, a fifth his Judgment are rejected as apocryphal.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He wrote two epistles which are called Catholic, the second of which, on account of its difference from the first in style, is considered by many not to be by him.
quotes.note: In his biographical catalog of Christian writers, Jerome affirms that Peter wrote two Catholic epistles, noting the stylistic debates surrounding the second while distinguishing both from five rejected apocryphal Petrine works.

quotes.quote: The apostles James, Peter, John, and Jude, have published seven epistles at once spiritual and to the point, short and long, short that is in words but lengthy in substance so that there are few indeed who do not find themselves in the dark when they read them. The apocalypse of John has as many mysteries as words. In saying this I have said less than the book deserves. All praise of it is inadequate; manifold meanings lie hidden in its every word.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The apostles James, Peter, John, and Jude, have published seven epistles at once spiritual and to the point
quotes.note: Writing from Bethlehem to Paulinus of Nola inside his complete survey of the biblical books, Jerome groups both Petrine letters within the seven apostolic Catholic Epistles of the New Testament.

Augustine of Hippo.apostolic_link: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church.
Augustine of Hippo.note: Bishop of Hippo; towering theologian and biblical doctor of the Western Church. — Hippo Regius, North Africa

quotes.quote: The authority of the Old Testament is contained within the limits of these forty-four books. That of the New Testament, again, is contained within the following:— Four books of the Gospel, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul — one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, to Philemon, to the Hebrews: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one of the Revelation of John.
quotes.highlight_phrase: two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James;
quotes.note: Enumerating the authoritative New Testament canon for the Western church in AD 397, Augustine of Hippo explicitly includes two epistles of Peter alongside the Pauline letters, Gospels, Acts, and Revelation.

Council of Carthage.apostolic_link: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine.
Council of Carthage.note: Plenary council of North African bishops attended by Augustine. — Carthage, North Africa

works.title: Canons of the Council of Carthage

quotes.quote: Item, that besides the Canonical Scriptures nothing be read in church under the name of divine Scripture. But the Canonical Scriptures are as follows: Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy. Joshua the Son of Nun. The Judges. Ruth. The Kings, iv. books. The Chronicles, ij. books. Job. The Psalter. The Five books of Solomon. The Twelve Books of the Prophets. Isaiah. Jeremiah. Ezechiel. Daniel. Tobit. Judith. Esther. Ezra, ij. books. Macchabees, ij. books. The New Testament. The Gospels, iv. books. The Acts of the Apostles, j. book. The Epistles of Paul, xiv. The Epistles of Peter, the Apostle, ij. The Epistles of John the Apostle, iij. The Epistles of James the Apostle, j. The Epistle of Jude the Apostle, j. The Revelation of John, j. book. Let this be sent to our brother and fellow bishop, Boniface, and to the other bishops of those parts, that they may confirm this canon, for these are the things which we have received from our fathers to be read in church.
quotes.highlight_phrase: The Epistles of Peter, the Apostle, ij.
quotes.note: Representing the North African episcopate at the Council of Carthage in AD 397, this conciliar decree formally ratifies two epistles of the Apostle Peter for liturgical reading as canonical Scripture.

Rufinus of Aquileia.apostolic_link: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius.
Rufinus of Aquileia.note: Latin scholar, historian, and translator of Origen and Eusebius. — Aquileia & Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: Of the New there are four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle, one of Jude, three of John, the Revelation of John. These are the books which the Fathers have comprised within the Canon, and from which they would have us deduce the proofs of our faith.
quotes.highlight_phrase: fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, two of the Apostle Peter, one of James, brother of the Lord and Apostle
quotes.note: Writing in northern Italy at the close of the fourth century, Rufinus of Aquileia records two epistles of the Apostle Peter within the received New Testament canon inherited from the Fathers.

book_meta.author_role: Apostle and Eyewitness Disciple of Christ

internal_evidence.summary: Opens with an emphatic physical eyewitness testimony: 'What we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of Life' (1 John 1:1).

verse_details.text: What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and touched with our hands, concerning the Word of Life--
what we have seen and heard we proclaim to you also, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father, and with His Son Jesus Christ.
We have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son [to be] the Savior of the world.
These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: None; 1 John's Johannine authorship is widely accepted across critical and conservative scholarship.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Polycarp of Smyrna quotes 1 John 4:2–3 in Phil 7:1; universally received in the Muratorian Canon, Irenaeus, Clement, Tertullian, and categorized by Eusebius as an undisputed Homologoumenon.

Papias of Hierapolis.apostolic_link: Hearer of the Apostle John and the Presbyter John; companion of Polycarp.
Papias of Hierapolis.note: Hearer of the Apostle John and the Presbyter John; companion of Polycarp. — Hierapolis, Asia Minor

works.title: Expositions of Oracles of the Lord (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: But concerning Matthew he writes as follows: So then Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able. And the same writer uses testimonies from the first Epistle of John and from that of Peter likewise.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the same writer uses testimonies from the first Epistle of John and from that of Peter likewise.
quotes.note: Preserved by Eusebius in his Church History, this testimony confirms that Papias, a direct hearer of the Apostle John, drew authoritative proofs from the First Epistle of John in the early second century.

quotes.quote: [This is what is related by Papias regarding Mark; but with regard to Matthew he has made the following statements]: Matthew put together the oracles [of the Lord] in the Hebrew language, and each one interpreted them as best he could. [The same person uses proofs from the First Epistle of John, and from the Epistle of Peter in like manner. And he also gives another story of a woman who was accused of many sins before the Lord, which is to be found in the Gospel according to the Hebrews.]
quotes.highlight_phrase: The same person uses proofs from the First Epistle of John, and from the Epistle of Peter in like manner.
quotes.note: Papias of Hierapolis, an early second-century hearer of the Apostle John in Asia Minor, provides the earliest explicit historical attestation to the circulation and authoritative use of the First Epistle of John.

Muratorian Fragment.apostolic_link: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome.
Muratorian Fragment.note: Roman canonical list composed shortly after Bishop Pius I of Rome. — Rome, Italy

quotes.quote: The fourth Gospel is that of John, one of the disciples. When his fellow disciples and bishops entreated him, he said, Fast now with me for the space of three days, and let us recount to each other whatever may be revealed to each of us. On the same night it was revealed to Andrew, one of the apostles, that John should narrate all things in his own name as they called them to mind. And hence, although different points are taught us in the several books of the Gospels, there is no difference as regards the faith of believers, inasmuch as in all of them all things are related under one imperial Spirit, which concern the Lord's nativity, His passion, His resurrection, His conversation with His disciples, and His twofold advent, — the first in the humiliation of rejection, which is now past, and the second in the glory of royal power, which is yet in the future. What marvel is it, then, that John brings forward these several things so constantly in his epistles also, saying in his own person, What we have seen with our eyes, and heard with our ears, and our hands have handled, that have we written. For thus he professes himself to be not only the eye- witness, but also the hearer; and besides that, the historian of all the wondrous facts concerning the Lord in their order.
quotes.highlight_phrase: John brings forward these several things so constantly in his epistles also, saying in his own person, What we have seen with our eyes
quotes.note: The second-century Muratorian Fragment links the Apostle John's authorship of the Fourth Gospel directly to his epistles, quoting the opening eyewitness declaration of 1 John 1:1 as John's own personal testimony.

Irenaeus of Lyons.apostolic_link: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John).
Irenaeus of Lyons.note: Disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who was taught directly by the Apostle John). — Lyons, Gaul & Smyrna

quotes.quote: The Gospel, therefore, knew no other son of man but Him who was of Mary, who also suffered; and no Christ who flew away from Jesus before the passion; but Him who was born it knew as Jesus Christ the Son of God, and that this same suffered and rose again, as John, the disciple of the Lord, verifies, saying: But these are written, that you might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you might have eternal life in His name, — foreseeing these blasphemous systems which divide the Lord, as far as lies in their power, saying that He was formed of two different substances. For this reason also he has thus testified to us in his Epistle: Little children, it is the last time; and as you have heard that Antichrist does come, now have many antichrists appeared; whereby we know that it is the last time. They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us: but [they departed], that they might be made manifest that they are not of us. Know therefore, that every lie is from without, and is not of the truth. Who is a liar, but he that denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is Antichrist.
quotes.highlight_phrase: as John, the disciple of the Lord, verifies
quotes.note: Writing in Gaul after learning from Polycarp in Asia Minor, Irenaeus explicitly identifies John, the disciple of the Lord, as the author of both the Fourth Gospel and the First Epistle of John.

Clement of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen.
Clement of Alexandria.note: Pupil of Pantaenus; head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; teacher of Origen. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: That which was from the beginning; which we have seen with our eyes; which we have heard. Following the Gospel according to John, and in accordance with it, this Epistle also contains the spiritual principle.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Following the Gospel according to John, and in accordance with it, this Epistle also contains the spiritual principle.
quotes.note: In his commentary fragments on the Catholic Epistles, Clement of Alexandria quotes the opening verse of 1 John and connects its theological teaching directly to the Gospel according to John.

quotes.quote: John, too, manifestly teaches the differences of sins, in his larger Epistle, in these words: If any man see his brother sin a sin that is not unto death, he shall ask, and he shall give him life: for these that sin not unto death, he says. For there is a sin unto death: I do not say that one is to pray for it. All unrighteousness is sin; and there is a sin not unto death.
quotes.highlight_phrase: John, too, manifestly teaches the differences of sins, in his larger Epistle
quotes.note: Teaching in late second-century Alexandria, Clement explicitly cites 1 John 5:16-17 as the Apostle John's "larger Epistle," demonstrating early awareness of multiple Johannine letters alongside the First Epistle.

Tertullian.apostolic_link: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church.
Tertullian.note: Father of Latin theology; defender of the apostolic rule of faith in the Western Church. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: From the Epistle also of John they immediately cull (a proof ). It is said: The blood of His Son purifies us utterly from every sin. Always then, and in every form, we will sin, if always and from every sin He utterly purifies us; or else, if not always, not again after believing; and if not from sin, not again from fornication. But what is the point whence (John) has started? He had predicated God to be Light, and that darkness is not in Him, and that we lie if we say that we have communion with Him, and walk in darkness. If, however, he says, we walk in the light, we shall have communion with Him, and the blood of Jesus Christ our Lord purifies us utterly from every sin.
quotes.highlight_phrase: From the Epistle also of John they immediately cull (a proof ).
quotes.note: Writing from Carthage in the early third century, Tertullian cites the First Epistle of John as an established apostolic authority within North African ecclesiastical debates over penitential discipline.

quotes.quote: But the fearful, says John — and then come the others — will have their part in the lake of fire and brimstone. Thus fear, which, as stated in his epistle, love drives out, has punishment.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Thus fear, which, as stated in his epistle, love drives out, has punishment.
quotes.note: In his early third-century treatise defending Christian martyrdom in Carthage, Tertullian links John's teaching on love casting out fear in his epistle directly with the Apostle's Apocalypse.

quotes.quote: John, however, in the Apocalypse is charged to chastise those who eat things sacrificed to idols, and who commit fornication. There are even now another sort of Nicolaitans. Theirs is called the Gaian heresy. But in his epistle he especially designates those as Antichrists who denied that Christ had come in the flesh, and who refused to think that Jesus was the Son of God.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But in his epistle he especially designates those as Antichrists who denied that Christ had come in the flesh
quotes.note: Tertullian attests in early third-century North Africa that the same Apostle John who wrote the Apocalypse also authored the epistle warning the Church against docetic antichrists.

Origen of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius.
Origen of Alexandria.note: Head of the Catechetical Schools of Alexandria and Caesarea; confessor under Decius. — Alexandria, Egypt & Caesarea, Palestine

works.title: Commentary on the Gospel of John

quotes.quote: And in his Catholic Epistle John says that He is a Paraclete for our souls with the Father, as thus: And if any one sin, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he adds that He is a propitiation for our sins, and similarly Paul says He is a propitiation: Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in His blood, on account of forgiveness of the forepast sins, in the forbearance of God. According to Paul, too, He is declared to be the wisdom and the power of God, as in the Epistle to the Corinthians: Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. It is added that He is also sanctification and redemption: He was made to us of God, he says, wisdom and righteousness and sanctification and redemption. But he also teaches us, writing to the Hebrews, that Christ is a High-Priest: Having, therefore, a great High-Priest, who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And in his Catholic Epistle John says that He is a Paraclete for our souls with the Father
quotes.note: Writing in Alexandria during the early third century, Origen explicitly designates First John as the Apostle's Catholic Epistle and places its Christological teaching alongside Paul's letters.

quotes.quote: It is of His last baptism, as some hold, that He speaks in the words, I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I straitened till it be accomplished? And it agrees with this that the disciple John speaks in his Epistle of the Spirit, and the water, and the blood, as being one.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the disciple John speaks in his Epistle of the Spirit, and the water, and the blood, as being one.
quotes.note: Origen explicitly identifies the author of First John as the disciple John, attesting to the epistle's early reception and Johannine attribution in third-century Alexandria.

quotes.quote: I know that some will attempt to say that, even according to the declarations of our own Scriptures, God is a body, because in the writings of Moses they find it said, that our God is a consuming fire; and in the Gospel according to John, that God is a Spirit, and they who worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth. Fire and spirit, according to them, are to be regarded as nothing else than a body. Now, I should like to ask these persons what they have to say respecting that passage where it is declared that God is light; as John writes in his Epistle, God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.
quotes.highlight_phrase: as John writes in his Epistle, God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.
quotes.note: In his foundational systematic treatise composed in Alexandria, Origen cites the First Epistle of John alongside the Fourth Gospel as authoritative apostolic Scripture defining the incorporeal nature of God.

works.title: Expositions of John's Gospel (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: In the fifth book of his Expositions of John's Gospel, he speaks thus concerning the epistles of the apostles: But he who was 'made sufficient to be a minister of the New Testament, not of the letter, but of the Spirit,' that is, Paul, who 'fully preached the Gospel from Jerusalem and round about even unto Illyricum,' did not write to all the churches which he had instructed and to those to which he wrote he sent but few lines. And Peter, on whom the Church of Christ is built, 'against which the gates of hell shall not prevail,' has left one acknowledged epistle; perhaps also a second, but this is doubtful. Why need we speak of him who reclined upon the bosom of Jesus, John, who has left us one Gospel, though he confessed that he might write so many that the world could not contain them? And he wrote also the Apocalypse, but was commanded to keep silence and not to write the words of the seven thunders. He has left also an epistle of very few lines; perhaps also a second and third; but not all consider them genuine, and together they do not contain hundred lines.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He has left also an epistle of very few lines; perhaps also a second and third
quotes.note: Writing in early third-century Alexandria and Caesarea, Origen catalogs the New Testament writings and affirms that the Apostle John, who reclined on Jesus' bosom, left the Fourth Gospel and an undisputed First Epistle.

Cyprian of Carthage.apostolic_link: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian.
Cyprian of Carthage.note: Bishop of Carthage and leader of the North African church; martyr under Valerian. — Carthage, North Africa

quotes.quote: The Lord, when, after His resurrection, He sent forth His apostles, charges them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. And the Apostle John, remembering this charge, subsequently lays it down in his epistle: Hereby, says he, we do know that we know Him, if we keep His commandments. He that says he knows Him, and keeps not His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
quotes.highlight_phrase: And the Apostle John, remembering this charge, subsequently lays it down in his epistle
quotes.note: As Bishop of Carthage in the mid-third century, Cyprian explicitly attributes the epistle to the Apostle John, connecting its moral exhortations directly to Christ's commission to the Twelve.

quotes.quote: For that he who is jealous of his brother, and has him in hatred, is bound by the guilt of homicide, the Apostle John declares in his epistle, saying, Whosoever hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that no murderer has life abiding in him. And again: He that says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now, and walks in darkness, and knows not whither he goes, because that darkness has blinded his eyes.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the Apostle John declares in his epistle, saying, Whosoever hates his brother is a murderer
quotes.note: Writing in mid-third-century North Africa, Cyprian of Carthage cites the First Epistle of John by name as binding apostolic instruction from the Apostle John on Christian ethics.

works.title: Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews

quotes.quote: Also in the Epistle of John: Every spirit which confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God. But whosoever denies that He has come in the flesh is not of God, but is of the spirit of Antichrist.
quotes.highlight_phrase: Also in the Epistle of John: Every spirit which confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God.
quotes.note: In his mid-third-century manual of Scriptural testimonies compiled in Carthage, Cyprian places the Epistle of John alongside the Gospels and Pauline letters as canonical proof of the Incarnation.

Dionysius of Alexandria.apostolic_link: Bishop of Alexandria ('the Great'); pupil of Origen.
Dionysius of Alexandria.note: Bishop of Alexandria ('the Great'); pupil of Origen. — Alexandria, Egypt

quotes.quote: That this person was called John, therefore, and that this was the writing of a John, I do not deny. And I admit further, that it was also the work of some holy and inspired man. But I could not so easily admit that this was the apostle, the son of Zebedee, the brother of James, and the same person with him who wrote the Gospel which bears the title according to John, and the catholic epistle. But from the character of both, and the forms of expression, and the whole disposition and execution of the book, I draw the conclusion that the authorship is not his. For the evangelist nowhere else subjoins his name, and he never proclaims himself either in the Gospel or in the epistle.
quotes.highlight_phrase: the apostle, the son of Zebedee, the brother of James, and the same person with him who wrote the Gospel which bears the title according to John, and the catholic epistle
quotes.note: Dionysius of Alexandria explicitly identifies the author of the Fourth Gospel and the First Catholic Epistle as the Apostle John, the son of Zebedee and brother of James.

works.title: On the Promises (preserved in Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica))
works.preserving_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History (Historia Ecclesiastica)

quotes.quote: But John never speaks as if referring to himself, or as if referring to another person. But the author of the Apocalypse introduces himself at the very beginning: 'The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which he gave him to show unto his servants quickly; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John, who bore witness of the word of God and of his testimony, even of all things that he saw.' 10. Then he writes also an epistle: 'John to the seven churches which are in Asia, grace be with you, and peace.' But the evangelist did not prefix his name even to the Catholic Epistle; but without introduction he begins with the mystery of the divine revelation itself: 'That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes.' For because of such a revelation the Lord also blessed Peter, saying, 'Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed it unto you, but my heavenly Father.' 11. But neither in the reputed second or third epistle of John, though they are very short, does the name John appear; but there is written the anonymous phrase, 'the elder.' But this author did not consider it sufficient to give his name once and to proceed with his work; but he takes it up again: 'I, John, who also am your brother and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and in the patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos for the Word of God and the testimony of Jesus.' And toward the close he speaks thus: 'Blessed is he that keeps the words of the prophecy of this book, and I, John, who saw and heard these things.' 12. But that he who wrote these things was called John must be believed, as he says it; but who he was does not appear. For he did not say, as often in the Gospel, that he was the beloved disciple of the Lord, or the one who lay on his breast, or the brother of James, or the eyewitness and hearer of the Lord. 13. For he would have spoken of these things if he had wished to show himself plainly. But he says none of them; but speaks of himself as our brother and companion, and a witness of Jesus, and blessed because he had seen and heard the revelations.
quotes.highlight_phrase: But the evangelist did not prefix his name even to the Catholic Epistle; but without introduction he begins with the mystery of the divine revelation itself
quotes.note: Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria provides a detailed third-century philological analysis affirming that the Evangelist John composed the Catholic Epistle beginning at 1 John 1:1 without needing to prefix his own name.

Eusebius of Caesarea.apostolic_link: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history.
Eusebius of Caesarea.note: Bishop of Caesarea; pupil of the martyr Pamphilus; father of Church history. — Caesarea, Palestine

quotes.quote: Since we are dealing with this subject it is proper to sum up the writings of the New Testament which have been already mentioned. First then must be put the holy quaternion of the Gospels; following them the Acts of the Apostles. After this must be reckoned the epistles of Paul; next in order the extant former epistle of John, and likewise the epistle of Peter, must be maintained. After them is to be placed, if it really seem proper, the Apocalypse of John, concerning which we shall give the different opinions at the proper time. These then belong among the accepted writings. Among the disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many, are extant the so-called epistle of James and that of Jude, also the second epistle of Peter, and those that are called the second and third of John, whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name.
quotes.highlight_phrase: next in order the extant former epistle of John, and likewise the epistle of Peter, must be maintained
quotes.note: In his landmark fourth-century catalog of the New Testament canon, Eusebius of Caesarea places the First Epistle of John among the universally acknowledged writings accepted throughout the Church.

quotes.quote: But of the writings of John, not only his Gospel, but also the former of his epistles, has been accepted without dispute both now and in ancient times. But the other two are disputed.
quotes.highlight_phrase: of the writings of John, not only his Gospel, but also the former of his epistles, has been accepted without dispute both now and in ancient times
quotes.note: Surveying the library and traditions of the early Church at Caesarea, Eusebius testifies that the Apostle John's First Epistle was accepted without dispute by both ancient and contemporary Christians.

quotes.quote: He states these things concerning the Apocalypse in the work referred to. He also mentions the first Epistle of John, taking many proofs from it, and likewise the first Epistle of Peter.
quotes.highlight_phrase: He also mentions the first Epistle of John, taking many proofs from it
quotes.note: Eusebius of Caesarea documents how second-century bishop Irenaeus of Lyons repeatedly cited the First Epistle of John as authoritative Scripture across his theological treatises.

internal_evidence.summary: The Elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, warning against deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.

verse_details.text: The elder to the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in truth; and not only I, but also all who know the truth,
For many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who do not acknowledge Jesus Christ [as] coming in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the antichrist.
Though I have many things to write to you, I do not want to [do so] with paper and ink; but I hope to come to you and speak face to face, so that your joy may be made full.

scholarly_discussion.critical_objection: Some ancient and modern scholars noted the self-designation 'the Elder' rather than 'the Apostle'.
scholarly_discussion.historical_evaluation: Peter likewise calls himself 'fellow elder' in 1 Peter 5:1; Irenaeus explicitly quotes 2 John 7–8 in Against Heresies (I.16.3; III.16.8) as the work of John the disciple of the Lord, and the Muratorian Canon includes two epistles of John.

quotes.quote: But John never speaks as if referring to himself, or as if referring to another person. But the author of the Apocalypse introduces himself at the very beginning: 'The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which he gave him to show unto his servants quickly; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John, who bore witness of the word of God and of his testimony, even of all things that he saw.' 10. Then he writes also an epistle: 'John to the seven churches which are in Asia, grace be with you, and peace.' But the evangelist did not prefix his name even to the Catholic Epistle; but without introduction he begins with the mystery of the divine revelation itself: 'That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes.' For because of such a revelation the Lord also blessed Peter, saying, 'Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed it unto you, but my heavenly Father.' 11. But neither in the reputed second or third epistle of John, though they are very short, does the name John appear; but there is written the anonymous phrase, 'the elder.' But this author did not consider it sufficient to give his name once and to proceed with his work; but he takes it up again: 'I, John, who also am your brother and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and in the patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos for the Word of God and the testimony of Jesus.' And toward the close he speaks thus: 'Blessed is he that keeps the words of the prophecy of this book, and I, John, who saw and heard these things.' 12. But that he who wrote these things was called John must be believed, as he says it; but who he was does not appear. For he did not say, as often in the Gospel, that he was the beloved disciple of the Lord, or the one who lay on his breast, or the brother of James, or the eyewitness and hearer of the Lord. 13. For he would have spoken of these things if he had wished to show himself plainly. But he says none of them; but speaks of himself as our brother and companion, and a witness of Jesus, and blessed because he had seen and heard the revelations.

After them is to be placed, if it really seem proper, the Apocalypse of John, concerning which we shall give the different opinions at the proper time. These then belong among the accepted writings.
